data.organization: Institute of the Industrial Ecology Problems of the North of Kola Science Center of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
data.notes:
Updated Apr 2017 (specialty, correspondent, important collections updated).

There are three collections in the herbarium. The main collection contains vascular plants (1500 specimens), fungi (1600 specimens), lichens (500 specimens) and bryophytes (1320 specimens)  from the Murmansk Region and other northern regions. Additionally, the Museum of Bacteria, Algae and Microfungi of the Kola Peninsula includes strains of bacteria (37), algae (200) and microfungi (395) isolated from soils (virgin and polluted by industrial emissions of the «Severonikel» and the «Pechenganikel» enterprises, of the aluminium plant, oil-contaminated), air and anthropogenically altered environment (apatite-nepheline ore, nepheline sands, circulating water of mining plant and others) of Kola Peninsula. Another special collection, Diatoms of the Euro-Arctic Region, includes specimens of diatom complexes from the sediments and biotopes from polytypic ancient and modern water bodies, periphyton and plankton of Euro-Arctic Region: Kola Peninsula (Imandra Lake, River Paz system, mountain lakes and rivers of Khibiny and Chuna-tundra massifs and others), Arkhangelsk region (River Pechora basin), lakes and streams of Novaya Zemlya Island, Svalbard archipelago, Barents, Norwegian, Greenland and Laptev’s Seas. This collection, founded in 1993, contains 150 different specimens (about 3700 slides).
First volume of the Fungi Exsiccates from Murmansk Region issued in 2016. The present fascicule includes labels of 15 species: Amylostereum chailletii, Asterodon ferruginosus, Ceraceomyces serpens, Cerioporus mollis, Ceriporiopsis mucida, Clavaria fragilis, Laurilia sulcata, Laxitextum bicolor, Ramariopsis subtilis, Oxyporus populinus, Phellinus laevigatus, Sistotrema confluens, Skeletocutis stellae, Veluticeps abietina, Xanthoporus syringae.

Available: Some Plants of the Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), Luzon, Philippines

The UP Baguio herbarium started as a student herbarium. It used to be very small with few collections from students and faculty researchers. At present, the herbarium has grown and is focused on keeping representative collections of the flora of the Cordillera Administrative Region, Luzon, Philippines. It is presently the only herbarium in the Region hence many students and researchers use the facility for the identification and verification of their plants for their studies.

The herbarium is active in the collection of plants from various parts of the Cordillera. 

The herbarium will be transferred to a new building, the Biodiversity Center of the Cordillera, in the future when the building will have been constructed. There is also a plan for establishing a database of all the collections which will be shared on line. The main constraint of the herbarium is funding to develop and improve it further. There is no library yet and the meager books are the personal collections of the person in charge.

The herbarium is open for donations of taxonomic books and other related literature and materials.

Updated Nov 2017. The original OC collections (180,000  specimens) were transferred to MU (150,000 non-Ohio specimens) in 1967 and to OS (30,000 Ohio specimens) in the early 1990s.  OC was relaunched in 2017 with an entirely new collection of approximately 4,000 specimens.

Updated Nov 2017. The herbarium was presented to Stonyhurst College in 1898 by James Ward’s son, also James (educated at Stonyhurst from 1860 onwards). The notes relating to the gift state that James Ward began collecting for his British herbarium in 1825, and by 1871 had amassed 1,753 specimens. There is a second herbarium described as ‘Exotic’ which features specimens from Ireland and Switzerland, these last were collected in 1864. The Exotic Herbarium is described as being of the same size as the British. They are described using the Linnaean system. The collection is housed separately from the other Scientific collections, and is in the same folders and order as when it was donated in c1898. It has, to the best of my knowledge, never been examined by specialists and there is no catalogue or database of the Herbarium.

Updated Aug 2017 (large general update).  Implanted in the 70s under the coordination of Normélia Cláudia de Vasconcelos, the Herbarium of the Federal University of Pará (HF), originally belonging to the Department of Pharmacy, was transferred to the research building of the Institute of Biological Sciences (ICB) and later to the annex building of the ICB where it is currently.   It is mainly intended for didactic and pedagogical activities, mainly for undergraduate courses in Biological Sciences, but also receives material from collections of practical activities from other institutes. Teaching and extension projects, coordinated by UFPA botany teachers and with the participation of trainee students resulted in an increase in the number of exsicates, as well as the introduction of fruits, seeds (carpoteca) and flow! ers, deposited in alcohol for conservation. Currently, the herbarium has a collection of approximately 3,271 samples, belonging to 51 botanical orders and 151 families. As it has not yet been possible to catalog and update all the specimens (this procedure is being done with the help of students), we still do not know how many genera and species the herbarium has. At present, the curator of the Herbarium is the responsibility of  Dra. Roberta Macedo Cerqueira (Systematics and Plant Ecology Laboratory), who assumed this commitment at the end of August 2016. After changing the Herbarium curator, the order data, families and genera began to be updated for the classifications adopted by the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group (APG), which considers both molecular, morphological and anatomical data among others for the taxonomic classification of plants (the classification system previously adopted in the herbarium was the Engler System).

updated Jul 2012.  

Loans: Types not sent on loan.

History and specificity:

Initiated at the beginning of the 19th century, now with about 250 000 samples, this collection reflects: 1) the history of Marseille: port open to the world, especially to the former French overseas territories and 2) the competence and influence of the 19th century Provençal naturalists. Today this herbarium includes: currently active herbaria, historical collections of the 19th and the 20th century of the South-East of the France and various herbaria relating to France's colonial history.

Currently active herbaria: 1) a general world herbarium of vascular plants initiated by Louis Castagne in 1820, 2) a general herbarium of vascular plants of France, 3) a general herbarium of vascular plants of the French Mediterranean area, 4) a cytogenetic herbarium of plants mainly collected and studied by J. Contandriopoulos and R. Verlaque, 5) a general world herbarium of lichen and 6) a general world herbarium of bryophyte.
Historical and prestigious collections of the 19th and the 20th century of the South-East of the France, corresponding to the first "modern" flora : 1) Herbier Louis Castagne (Catalogue des plantes qui croissent naturellement dans le département des Bouches-du-Rhône), 2) Honoré Ardoino (Flore analytique du département des Alpes-maritimes), 3) Honoré Roux (Catalogue des plantes de Provence spontanées ou généralement cultivées)… Various herbaria relating to France's colonial history : 1) Herbier Père Antoine Duss des Antilles (Flore phanérogamique des Antilles françaises, Guadeloupe et Martinique), 2) Herbier Henri Jumelle and Henri Perrier de la Bathie for Madagascar (numerous publications among the Catalogue des plantes de Madagascar), 3) Herbier Eugène Jacob de Cordemoy for La Réunion (Flore de l'Ile de la Réunion), used for the " Flore des Mascareignes ", 4) Herbier Georg. Zenker (Cameroun), Herbier Boery (Mauritanie) for the " Afrique Orientale Française ", 5) Herbier Pennel and Metzger for the Nouvelle Calédonie.

Moreover, the botanical collections of the University include the Musée Colonial de Marseille founded in 1893 as a part of the Institut Colonial de Marseille. This collection contains plant samples from overseas selected and used for food (fruits, vegetables, cereals, oils, etc.), as condiments and spices, for pharmaceuticals and for industry (rubber, wood, fibres, etc.).
Updated Jul 2012.  The herbarium consists of significant endemic species as per IUCN criteria. It also supported by relevant literature, photoes and  live species in the Botanical Gardens.

data.notes: Entered Aug 2017.  The Highlands Biological Station Herbarium houses a significant southern Appalachian collection including material from NC and TN from 1875-1902, the Wheeler collection from the defunct Biltmore herbarium of about 200 specimens (1897-1900), collections from the Great Smoky Mountains (1930), extensive regional collections by Radford et al. (1950-1965) during preparation of the manual 'The Vascular Plants of the Carolinas,' and local collections contributed by staff, researchers, and course instructors working at HBS from the 1960s to the present.

Entered Aug 2017.  The collection has >2,000 specimens, dating back to the 1960s. Specimens have been collected from approximately 30 states. We also have Cuban specimens of the late, great euphorb expert Grady Webster.

Entered Aug 2017. The Herbarium MAR has a recent foundation date, July 2013, but it has a collection of plants that have been collected since 1980 in the State of Maranhão. Although recently, the collection is increasing due to developing undergraduate and postgraduate studies. It has records of plants of dune and restinga areas, as well as ecotonal environments that are a particular characteristic of Maranhão State. A collection of the families Sapotaceae, Myrtaceae, Poaceae, Arecaceae, Solanaceae, Asteraceae, Rubiaceae, Convolvulaceae and Cactaceae; And a collection of the areas belonging to the Maranhão Amazon is beginning  to expand the records of the species of the Northeast of Brazil.
Updated Sep 2017 (address, specimen total, correspondent).  The herbarium cases were moved along with the rest of the institution to Beckley in the past year.  The collection is being catalogued.

data.notes: Entered Feb 2016. The Montana State University Northern Herbarium represents a new repository for plants growing in the diverse habitats associated with this geographical area.  In addition to grass- and shrub lands, we house specimen vouchers from localized mountain areas that rise above the plains (e.g., Sweetgrass Hills, Bears Paw and Little Belt Mountains).  Plants collected from prairie potholes and limestone outcrops, as well as those from cottonwood dominated riparian areas and gumbo bluffs associated with the Missouri River Breaks, are included in the collection.  Voucher age ranges from the early 1900’s to the present and some of these represent plants collected from more well-known regions, e.g., Yellowstone, Rocky Mountain, and Glacier National Parks.

data.notes:
Entered Jul 2016.  The herbarium was established in 1987 with the foundation of the laboratory for plant resources of the Kamchatka Division of the Pacific Geographical Institute, FEB RAS (today, this laboratory is called: Laboratory for Plant Ecology of the Kamchatka Branch of the Pacific Geographical Institute). The herbarium contains collections of vascular plants, mosses, lichens, and fungi that have been compiled by members of the Kamchatka Division PGI FEB RAS as well as by scientists from associated organizations during floristic and geobotanical field studies on the Kamchatka peninsula and its adjacent regions and islands. As of today, 6100 specimens have been catalogued. The remaining 1640 specimens are the reference collection for the “Flora of the Russian Far East (Flora Exsicata) by Charkevich and Buch (1999). Digitizing and cataloging of the Flora Exsicata specimens is in progress.

data.notes:
Entered Mar 2016.  The Oman Botanic Garden, a unique project not only within Oman but the entire Arabian Peninsula, is currently under construction. It aims to present and showcase the native flora and habitats of the country to visitors and offers student, researchers and other botanic gardens (national and international) modern facilities and expertise in a state of the art research centre.    The OBG herbarium will be a major focus of the research centre. The herbarium is currently working closely with researchers from within Oman (e.g. Sultan Qaboos University) and international research institutions (e.g. Royal Botanic Gardens of Edinburgh). 

Oman’s native flora consists of approximately 1408 species, distributed within highly diverse habitats throughout the country. Remote and inaccessible areas of the country have yet to be studied. There is a relatively high possibility that new plant records will be discovered during the course of OBG’s field collecting trips.
 
Although we are at the beginning of a large task, the OBG herbarium collection is constantly growing and aims at increasing our specimen numbers vastly within the next two to three years.  On our many field trips throughout Oman, collecting herbarium vouchers is of critical importance. Of nearly all the species collected so far, multiple vouchers are available. The wide range of morphological variation within and between Oman’s diverse habitats is captured for many of the species. Vouchers of rare and endemic species are included in our collection as well.

In Oman, we are so far the only herbarium/institution that regularly undertakes scientific curation and physical curation inspections by trained staff and documents all procedures

Updated Apr 2014.  The Elizabeth Teter Lunn Herbarium is home to more than 5,000 plant specimens dating primarily from the turn of the twentieth century, with some being collected, purportedly, as early as 1848. Between the years 1895 and 1897. M.C. Jensen, a student and botanist, collected more than 80 specimens within the city of Lake Forest, IL, and added these to the College's collection.  At present, student Victoria Jones is in the process of writing a proposal for Lake Forest College to pay more attention to the collection and thus salvage this one-of-a-kind herbarium. This proposal reflects Victoria's senior-thesis topic and all of the tedious curatorial work she has committed to for the past three years. Victoria is currently working alongside Gerould Wilhelm, the foremost vascular plant botanist of the Chicago Region, to observe truth and beauty in each specimen of the ETL Herbarium. The outcome will be Gerould Wilhelm's & Laura Rericha's brand new book, "Flora of the Chicago Region." This book will update Swink & Wilhelm's "Plants of the Chicago Region" (1994).

The majority of the collection contains specimens from Illinois Beach State Park (IBSP) collected by Elizabeth Teter Lunn (professor at Lake Forest College) between the 1950s and mid-1970s. Lunn's interest in collecting from IBSP was based on an earlier study tallying the park's flora during the 1900s. The result was the publication of her guidebook, "Plants of the Illinois Dunesland," completed in 1982 and published by The Illinois Dunesland Preservation Society.

The herbarium contains specimens of 150 families of flowering plants along with collections of gymnosperms (conifers) and lower plants (non-seed producing plants) and all of these plant species are entirely indigenous in nature. The collection is currently being digitized, and the herbarium staff building an electronic Herbarium Catalogue containing images of the specimens and information taken from their collection labels.  The overall objective of digitization of the herbarium is to link this national wealth of the country with international research institutes and global web of knowledge.  The oldest specimens were collected some 50 years ago and 52 per cent of all flowering plant genera are represented in the collection.
 
The herbarium scientists are committed to making this important collection more accessible to botanists and others, wherever they may be, for use in their own projects: particularly in biodiversity, conservation and sustainable development. Currently ongoing projects linked to herbarium include taxonomic studies of wild vegetables, wild edible fruits, biodiesel plants based resources, medicinal plants and pollen flora of Northern Pakistan.

data.notes:
Updated Oct 2015..  The herbarium was created because of the need of professors and students of having an appropriate space for the investigation and of the study of flora in the state. In its start-up was directed by professor Rafael Guarin Montoya with the help of  his auxiliary Mardoqueo Villarreal. In 1984 the management was in charge of professor Rafael Castillo.In 1998 he dismissed and only  at the beginning of 1999 professor Maria  Eugenia Morales Puentes took over the direction  and she is still in charge of the herbarium UPTC. The UPTC herbarium is a collection of regional type, registered as a biological collection with scientific  purposes before the institute Alexander Von Humboldt (number 26 under initial UPTC-H),According to legislation established by the Ministry of Environment in resolution number 1115 of year 2000 ,and it is considered National Patrimony, besides of being place of important reference of fauna an d flora from Boyaca ,although  it includes areas from sates that share borders as Casanare and Santander. The herbarium has about 21,314 specimen and some vegetal collections among them  the Briofitos collection(Mosses,Hepatics,Antoceros y Lichens), from Ferns and Licofitas of angioespermas from fruits and seeds(carpoteca) and a collection that has being created  nowadays referred to vegetal fibers.The logo of the herbarium is represented through an illustration  od Diplostephium jenesanum,a specie founded in the Boyaca State and it is described by the actual director and Santiago Diaz Piedrahita, sample type of the UPTC-H herbarium .
Nowadays the herbarium is an active member of  a variety  of museums in Boyaca , its capital Tunja and of course  of the university, besides  it is member of Colombian association of herbariums(ACH) and has agreements with different public and private institutions in the country. The herbarium has a future projection as a unit where an important collection of plants from Boyaca and the Eastern Cordillera can be deposit, focused to services and problem solving, hypothesis, consulting, among others thesis, master degrees  and PhD, visits to institutions (schools, universities and people interested in the matter)service of determination, drying and assembly of vegetal material, also we have a documentation center ,microscopy  area, specialized software area (canopy l, leaves and seeds),cartographies, projection area, also we advise services related to Botany  which are available to all the students and researchers.

Roos and other botanists between 1920 and 1990. A small collection of lichens and fungi was assembled during the 1930s by Edmund C. Jaeger, and was later donated to the Museum during his tenure as Curator of Plants. data.associatedHerbaria: Lewis Ginter Botanical Garden, 1800 Lakeside Ave. Rich VA 23228
data.notes:
Updated Feb 2016. The Lee Park Herbarium was begun in 1937 as part of a WPA project to create a wildflower sanctuary. In addition to clearing land and planting native plants, the WPA workers were taught to collect and preserve specimens.  This part of the collection comprises 325 specimens; collection ended about 1940.  In the 1990s, Donna M.E. Ware, botanist at the College of William and Mary, began collecting in Lee Park anew.  Her goal was to determine if the original 325 species still grew there, and then expanded her project to collect other plants in the Park and watershed.  The Ware portion of the herbariam comprises 800 specimens and collection continues on this portion.

The herbarium collection includes 238 corresponding watercolors exquisitely painted by Bessie Neimeyer Marshall during the depression era in the 1930’s.  The botanical renderings are showcased in With Paintbrush and Shovel: Preserving Virginia’s Wildflowers.

data.notes: Updated Jul 2017 (geocoordinates updated).  30 000 bryophytes and lichens of KRA on permanent loan to KRAM. Private herbarium of Jan Kornas and Anna Medwecka-Kornas (40 000 specimens) stored at KRA.  There are preserved also two historical herbaria of 18th century. The first is a book of 27 sheets (24,5 x 40 cm) with 172 specimens of plants labelled with pre-Linnean latin names. It was made by an unknown author after 1700. The second herbarium consists of four unified folio volumes (32 x 44,5 cm). The volume 1 includes 104 sheets, vol. 2 - 98, vol. 3 - 100, vol. 4 - 104 sheets and the herbarium contains 383 species of plants. After the title page the owner of the herbarium was ANDRZEJ BADURSKI (1740-1789), lecturer of medicine at Cracow University, educated at the University of Bologna. The herbarium was probably made under the supervision of GAETANO LORENZO MONTI (1712-1797), professor of medical botany at Bologna University.  The Paleobotanical collection, of the  Paleobotanic Museum , has a rich collection of over 150 thousand specimens of fossil plants (including microscopic preparations of the anatomy of certain plants) from all geological periods of Earth's history, from the Devonian period of the Holocene. The oldest exhibits date from the late XIX century (M. RACIBORSKI). One of the most valuable is a collection of Devonian first land plants. In the collection, there are several types of plants from the Devonian and Carboniferous period

data.associatedHerbaria: <Associated garden and institution:> Botanical Garden, Saint Petersburg State University. Biological Institute, Saint Petersburg State University, Peterhof branch.
data.notes:
Updated Oct 2017. 
Herbarium of the Botany Department of the Saint Petersburg State University (LECB) is one of the largest University Herbarium of Russia. Its funds contain at least 800,000 herbarium sheets of higher plants. Now Herbarium collection is unique in the structure of the University, both in historical and in scientific terms by geographical coverage and systematic collection of funds, the existing type specimens (more than 3,500 types in the present, as we found). The type collection includes quite a significant amount of rare and original authentic specimens collected by various botanists such as E. Boissier (1810–1885), V. Borbas (1844–1905), H. Cuming (1791–1865), A.P. Decandolle (1778–1841), J. Forster (1754–1794), W. Hooker (1785–1865), G. Schimper (1804–1878), V. Tineo (1791–1856), W. Besser (1784–1842), А. Bunge (1803–1890), R. Hohenacker (1798–1872), G. Karelin (1801–1872), I. Kirilov(1822–1842), St. Krasheninnikov (1711–1755), C. Ledebour (1785–1851), R. Maack (1825–1886), K. Meinshausen (1819–1899), C. Meyer (1795–1855), А. Nordmann (1803–1866), P. Pallas (1741–1811), Ch. Steven (1781–1863), N. Turzaninov (1793–1863), А. Shrenk (1816–1876) etc. 

This Herbarium is probably one of the oldest as Russia storage facilities. The oldest herbarium specimens kept in LECB, belong to the middle of XVII century, or even the end of XVI century. Prelinnean specimens found by us in G. Bongard (1786–1839) and E. Lindemann (1825–1901) collections. Thus, according to Lindemann, in his collection during his lifetime were kept for more than 60 specimens collected by prelinnean F. Ambrosi (2 sheets), J. Breyn (1637–1697) (36), C. Bauhin (1) (1560–1624), A. Clegero (1) (he collected Juniperus japonica from Japan in 1688), J. Gerard (1545–1612) (1), J. Gmelin (1709–1755) (20). Many specimens found in Bongard’s herbarium, but how many relics it contains is difficult to say, since Bongard did not kept accounting herbarium revenues. Currently LECB, revealed more than 60 prelinnean specimens. The most of them were found in herbaria Bongard – specimens belonged to J. Commelin (1629–1692), C. Commelin (1668–1731), Breyn, P. Hermann (1646–1695), G. Steller (1709–1746), Gmelin etc., as well as in the herbarium Lindemann to Bauhin, Clegero, Breyn, Gmelin, etc. Currently, the oldest specimen found in LECB, is a specimen of C. Bauhin (1560–1624) – Jucca gloriosa L., without an exact date on the label, but, undoubtedly, belonged to Bauhin. Some of the old specimens have only historical interest, other are syntypes for species of C. Linnaeus (1707–1778), P. Pallas (1741–1811), J. Lamarck (1744–1829) and others, which is why value these specimens is particularly large. Examples of these types: Melanthium sibiricum L., Anthericum calyculatum L., Convolvolus ammannii Desr., Convolvulus lineatus L., Yucca gloriosa L., Andromeda stelleriana Pall., Claytonia arctica Adam, Claytonia sibirica L., Alyssum hyperboreum L., Phlox sibirica L. Thus, LECB is the third in Russia after Moscow State University Herbarium (MW) and Komarov Botanical Institute RAS (LE), which revealed prelinnean specimens, and some of which refers to syntypes of Linnean taxa. 

Private herbaria of H. G. Bongard (25 000 specimens) and E. E. Lindemann (200 000 specimens) housed at LECB.

Two contributors to Bongard’s collection deserve special mention: Johann Jacob Boeber (1746-1820) and Carl Ludwig Willdenow (1765-1812). 

It was Boeber’s personal herbarium the first collection to have been acquired in 1823 by the Department of Botany and added to Bongard’s own collection, comprising at the time 6,783 species. According to Bongard, Boeber’s collection of 7,000 specimens, representing 6,000 vascular plants and 1,000 cryptogams, was for the most part “badly pressed, or damaged by use”. Subsequently, and for reasons unknown, most of its specimens had been transferred to the Botanical Museum and are presently kept at the Herbarium of the Komarov Botanical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences (LE). 

That Bongard’s collection at LECB includes some of Willdenow’s original specimens is not a widely known fact, either in Russia, or in the West. Our research indicates that there are 1,089 Willdenow’s specimens at LECB, with 104 of them authenticated by labels in his hand. This alone makes Bongard’s collection at LECB quite unique, both as a historic and scientific record. The only other Willdenow herbarium sheets in Russia, with labels in his hand, are found at LE (limited to algae), and at MW, the Moscow University Herbarium (about 50 sheets). 
Our preliminary study of Bongard’s collection at LECB identified around 1,450 type specimens (mostly syntypes and isotypes) that are currently kept in the Herbarium’s type collection of about 3,500 specimens. Among them, 42 type specimens of the Restionaceae, with 33 of them described by K.S. Kunth (1788-1850). Kunth, along with several other taxonomists, studied specimens collected by J.F. Drége (1794-1881) at the Cape of Good Hope and in other districts of the Cape Province in South Africa. There are also Bongard’s own type specimens, such as Соrallorhiza mertensiana Bong., collected by K.H. Mertens at Sitka, Alaska, with labels both in Bongard’s and Mertens’s hand. However, most of the types described by Bongard are kept at LE. The LECB specimens seem to be duplicates of those, with more detailed labels, found at LE.

data.notes: Entered Apr 2016.   Zion National Park manages a herbarium of over 3500 herbarium specimens.  Zion also manages the herbaria from Cedar Breaks National Monument, over 900 specimens, and Bryce Canon National Monument, over 1800 specimens.  These specimens provide baseline information about the natural environment of the three parks.  These collections display the remarkable diversity at the convergence of three ecological provinces: the Colorado Plateau, the Great Basin, and the Mojave Desert.  Zion’s collection represents over 95% of the confirmed 982 plant taxa in the park.  The earliest specimens in the herbaria were collected in the 1920s with additions to the collection continuing today. Most of the specimens were collected from 1950s to 1980s.

Entered Jul 2013. The ontogenetic herbarium is herbarium of plants of different stages of individual development. Ontogenetic states were revealed with the use of the concept of discrete description of ontogenesis taking into account morphological features-markers (table). The goal is to document every species in the Ontogenetic Herbariumwith specimens in different ontogenetic states from plantules to the senile plants (complete ontogenesis). Our Ontogenetic herbarium has duplicates of some species that we are ready to interchange, and we can also take herbarium of ontogenesis of any types of plants on storage. Exhibits in herbarium are arranged in alphabetical order of latin names of families and species inside these families. Systematic catalogue renovates constantly, the ontogenetic states of species, places of collections and main collectors are indicated in it.
The Ontogenetic herbarium in an accessible form for use, and  includes 5330 mounted sheets of  607 species of plants from 369 genera and 86 families, and also 1 lichen and 2 types of gymnospermous and higher cryptogams plants. It is used both in scientific and pedagogical aims.  The Ontogenetic Herbarium allows users to get skills of determination of ontogenetic states of plants of different biomorphes and to apply them for study and maintenance of population biodiversity. Today the Ontogenetic Herbarium is included in the department "Population-Ontogenetic Museum."

data.notes: Entered Oct 2010.  The Alfred Twining Herbarium is housed in two metal cabinets in the basement of the Everhart Museum.  The specimens are mounted on herbarium sheets or are loose in folders which are enclosed in additional folders and are arranged in a family sequence used by Alfred Twining in his <Flora of Northeastern Pennsylvania> (1917).  Most of the specimens were collected by Twining in the early twentieth centure prior to the publication of the flora.  EMNH is the major repository for Twining specimens -- few are duplicated at PH. The herbarium was established by  Bra native Federico Craven, co-founder of the museum, who between 1859 and 1880 collected and determined 622 species of vascular plants (862 specimens)   mainly coming from the immediate surroundings of his town. To it were added other collections of which the most important are as follows: F. Rota (1950 specimens.), and G. Abba (450 specimens). This material is kept in special drawers and periodically subjected to fumigation. Much of the herbarium is being cataloged, to  allow  for rapid on-line consultation of specific data collection and determination of each artifact.
The herbarium contains 300 specimens  of lichens,  552 specimens of  wood, a  spermatoteca collection of 350, and 300 succulent plants.

Entered Jul 2016.  The foci of the University of Malakand Botanic Garden and Herbarium are 1) conservation of the local flora both in- and ex-situ; 2) development of a herbarium emphasizing local species; 3) monographic study of local species, particularly those of high value medicinal plants; 4) DNA/Protein genotyping with an emphasis on local species; 5) tissue culture of rare local species to support their conservation and multiplication. The herbarium currently has about 2000 dry specimens from different localities in the Malakand division, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. More than 60% of the plants are endemic to Malakand division and acclimated to the environmental conditions of the botanic garden.

data.notes: Entered Jan 2012.  The Herbarium of Mordovian State Nature Reserve was  initially all  stored in one plywood cabinet. The fungi, lichens and mosses were stored in thick paper bags in a special plywood box. Today the herbarium collections of vascular plants Mordovian State Nature Reserve has 3216 herbarium sheets in 7 wooden cabinets, each of which is divided into 10 chambers, arranged in two columns.  The specimens are  arranged in the Englerian system.  Most of the herbarium collections were made within the reserve and in adjacent territories. The herbarium reflects  the species diversity of flora in the west of Mordovia, with  756 species belonging to 377 genera and 99 families.  The macrofungus herbarium has about 1500 specimens and includes about 400 species. It is stored in plastic ziplock bags enclosed in kraft paper bags and is located on the system, adopted in  the 9th edition of "Ainsworth and Bisbsy's Dictionary of the fungi". There are about  100 specimens of mosses, and about 700 specimens of lichens stored in cardboard boxes.

data.notes:
HUQ HISTORY:  
FOUNDERS: Germán Arbeláez Serna and María Cristina Vélez Nauer, professors of the Degree Program in Biology at the University of Quindío. This process was supported directly by SANTIAGO DIAZ PIEDRAHITA of the Herbarium COL.
HUQ INVESTIGATORS: Carlos Alberto Agudelo H., María del Pilar Sepúlveda, Germán Darío Gómez M., Andrés Felipe Orozco C., Ana Lucía López G., Rocío Stella Suárez, Ricardo Elías Vega, Carlos Alberto López R., Paula Andrea Viveros , Johan Carvajal, Larri Álvarez, Juan Fernando Restrepo, Carlos Alonso Maya, Rigoberto Villa, Rodolfo López, Nodier Augusto Botero, Jaime Uribe Meléndez, Neyver Rivera, Martha Chacón, among others. Among the administrative staff stands out Edier Flórez Henao.
PUBLICATIONS: HUQ researchers have published numerous publications (approximately 100) in journals such as Flora de Colombia (Asteraceae and Amaranthaceae), Caldasia (Amaranthaceae), Biological News, Novon, Catalogs (Flora de Antioquia and Flora de Venezuela), abstract books of scientific events, among others. Books on taxonomy of mosses, Euphorbiaceae, wax palm, flórulas of some localities, four volumes of the magazine Flora Andina, etc. There are also online publications such as the Amaranthaceae in Neotropical Flowering Plants at https://www.kew.org/science/tropamerica/neotropikey.htm.
YOUNG RESEARCHERS: At least 10 young Colombians, biologists and graduates in Biology, funded by COLCIENCIAS have passed through HUQ and have developed studies on flora, palynology, taxonomy, ecology, among others.
INTERNATIONAL TRAINERS: Several interns from Croatia, Slovenia, Portugal, Brazil and Austria have conducted training and learning about the Andean flora in HUQ.
INTERNATIONAL NETWORKS: The HUQ belongs to the Latin American Association of Botany - ALB, through Carlos A. Agudelo has participated as a member of the Superior Council of the ALB between 2010 and 2018, is also part of the Colombian Herbarium Association - ACH, of which he was President between 1998 and 1999 with Carlos A. Agudelo and is linked to the Global Initiative project of plants to type the world types in JSTOR through Felipe Orozco. We also work in a network with researchers from the University of Luján and La Matanza, Argentina through a binational agreement. With Venezuelan researchers participated in the elaboration of the New Catalog of the Flora of Venezuela, through Carlos A. Agudelo Amaranthaceae was reviewed for that country.
MASTERY IN SCIENCES VEGETABLE BIOLOGY: the HUQ collection, its literature and researchers were fundamental to propose the creation of the Master in 2002 before the Ministry of National Education of Colombia. Through this program 28 botanists have graduated and by 2018 there are 25 more active.
SCIENTIFIC EVENTS: The HUQ staff has carried out numerous local, regional, national and international scientific events (symposiums, congresses), courses, workshops, forums, diplomas (Organic Agriculture, protected areas and medicinal plants (the latter led by Orozco C., being very successful), botanical expeditions, have participated in the Latin American congresses of Botany of the ALB such as Cartagena in Colombia 2002, Santo Domingo in Dominican Republic 2006, La Serena in Chile 2010 and Salvador de Bahia in Brazil in 2014. The same They prepare to attend the XII Congress of Quito, Ecuador in 2018. They are part of the organizers of the biology regional symposiums held biannually among teachers from UTP, U. de Caldas, UNISARC and UniQuindío.

Nupélia herbarium currently has researchers as well as graduate students (UEM) and  PIBIC fellows  through CNPq and Araucaria Foundation,  and  volunteers and interns. The main objective of the collection is documenting  the riparian flora, including surveys, taxonomic identification and dissemination for both  the scientific and general communities, and to generate subsidies for ecological studies, conservation of biodiversity, land reclamation and sustainable development, particularly riparian areas of the Upper Paraná River floodplain. It is the database of various theses and dissertations related to floristic and phytosociological surveys and Phanerogams taxonomy. Functionally and structurally the herbarium  is linked to Nupélia. It is in computerization phase and available online by the Biological Collections Network of Paraná-Taxonline State and splink the CRIA. The herbarium is located in Block G-80 and open for consultation by experts appointment with coordination.

data.notes:
The main activities at TAN Herbarium are the following
- Conservation of herbarium 350 000 mounted specimens divided into 280 families, 1 885 genera and 8 745 species (2019)
- Inventory and collection of herbarium specimens
- Receipt of collected botanical samples from plant collectors
- Mandated by the Malagasy Government to receive the duplicate of specimens collected by foreign and national researchers before any specimens exportation.
- Digitizing and data-basing by using Botanical Research And Herbarium Management System (BRAHMS) software.
- Support tools for foreign and national researchers and high school students. 
- Assessment, review of conservation status of malagasy plants.
- Partnership with national institutions (Herbier TEF, DBEV and ENS) and international organizations (MBG, RBG Kew, CAS, HBV and IRD).
- Supervision of trainee students from public and private universities (on average 60 per year).

data.notes:
The accurate number of TAU specimens is not known, but it is estimated to c. 70,000. Each year at least 1,000 specimens are added. Most of the specimens come from Greece, but there are also several specimens from European countries and a few from other continents. The collections are divided in two sections: the new and the historical. 
The new collections include specimens of previous and current members of the Lab, as well as specimens of postgraduate students and doctoral candidates. Among them there are collections from: 
•	several mountainous areas and wetlands, mainly from Epirus, Macedonia and Thrace, including many areas of the NATURA 2000 network,
•	urban and rural areas,
•	a particularly rich collection of Lamiaceae plants

The historical collections of TAU hold more than 6,000 specimens, dating back from the early 19th century up to the late 30’s. Most come from the collections of Theodor von Heldreich, Theodore Orphanides, Joseph Sartori, Vasileios Tountas and Dimitrios Zaganiaris, as well as of many others.  There are at least 44 nomenclatural types, as well as many endemic and range restricted taxa. Perhaps the most valuable of the historical collections are those of Dimitrios Zaganiaris, which include more than 3,000 specimens and are kept, to the best of our knowledge, only in TAU.

data.notes: The Academy’s herbarium contains over 15,900 catalogued specimens, largely collected in the Midwest (58%), with a large proportion (60%) collected prior to 1900.  This portion of the herbarium contains mainly vascular plants, as well as some fungi (7%), bryophytes (1.5%), and algae (1.5%). Critically, the collection houses 19th century vouchers for six federally threatened and endangered species, including the sand dune thistle (Cirsium pitcheri) and the leafy prairie clover (Dalea foliosa), which are native to Great Lakes sand dune and Illinois prairie habitats. Just over 2,000 specimens from the Midwest have been digitally scanned and jpegs are available for research. The herbarium also contains a backlog of approximately 6,000 uncatalogued 19th century pressed plants. Nearly 90% of the backlog specimens are vascular plants collected in the Midwest and Great Lakes region.

data.notes:
Although only several years passed from the establishment of our Herbarium, we have actively tried to collect and document Iranian plant specimens over the past decade, especially vascular plants of the two large families, Asteraceae (genus Artemisia) and Amaryllidaceae (genus Allium). What is remarkable about our activities is that beside each Herbarium voucher we tried to collect also seed or living materials. Currently all these materials are preserved under optimal conditions in herbarium cabinets (dried sheets), refrigerators and/or freezers (usually seeds) or under cultivation in our living collections (bulbous or rhizomatous plants). We devoted an extra code (IBRC code) than herbarium numbers to each specimen to link easily different types of collected materials.     

Hitherto, our team had more than 300 working days mission our country wide to collect both herbarium and living material of special Iranian flora. In parallel to our Center policy, we are going to raise continuously our collections inventories. 

Recently, we decided to gradually digitize our determined and labeled sheets and put them available via internet. Interested researchers can see so far prepared specimens online via this internet address: http://ibrc.ir/index.aspx?fkeyid=&siteid=1&pageid=466&siteid=1
Entered Nov 2016.

data.notes:
The Troy University Herbarium (TROY) was established in 1954 as a teaching herbarium by Dr. Robert Dietz, who served as curator.  In 1961, the herbarium was moved from its original location in the basement of Bibb Graves Hall into the new science building, McCall Hall.  This 528 ft2 room served both as the herbarium and a paleobotany laboratory.  It remained in this location until 1988 when Dietz retired.  At that time, the herbarium was closed and all of the specimens were destroyed.  In 1997, the TROY Herbarium was reestablished by Dr. Alvin Diamond and Dr. Michael Woods.  In 1999, the collection had grown to approximately 3500 mounted specimens and the herbarium was moved to rooms 125 and 127 of the Math Science Complex (MSCX) (formally McCall Hall).  The two rooms totaled 443 ft2, which resulted in a 16% reduction in floor space from the previous location.  At the end of 2005, with 19 herbarium cabinets and a collection of approximately 19,000 mounted specimens, the herbarium had outgrown its space.  The Curators wrote a five-year plan for the herbarium and submitted it to the Troy University Administration.  With support of the Department Chair, Dean, Assistant Provost, and Provost, the herbarium was moved during 2006 to its current location, MSCX 216, which consists of 1058 ft2.  Since moving to its current location, the collection has grown to over 44,000 specimens with an average annual growth of over 2,000.  This makes TROY one of the fastest-growing herbarium in the southeastern United States.  Currently, 100 percent of all vascular plant specimens deposited in the TROY Herbarium have been databased and imaged.  Additionally, nonvascular plants have been databased. 

In 2017, the Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences (CAS) approved an additional 220 square foot room (MSCX 223) immediately across the hallway from the herbarium (MSCX 216).  This will allow us to relocate the plant dryer, freezer, mounting table, shelving for storage, filing cabinet for records pertaining to loans and exchanges, two data basing computers and imaging equipment to MSCX 223.  This will increase the safety of the collection by keeping all specimens outside of the herbarium until they have been processed and frozen.  
  All Alabama specimens are available on the Alabama Plant Atlas http://floraofalabama.org/

data.notes:
The Herbario Amazónico del Ecuador, ECUAMZ, is part of the Universidad Estatal Amazónica (UEA), a public university, the main campus of which is in Puyo, the capital of Pastaza province.  The herbarium is located  at the university`s research center, ""Centro de Investigación, Postgrado y Conservación Amazónica, known by the acronym CIPCA, 44 km  north of Puyo along the road to Tena (Ecuador highway 45, kilometer 319).  The CIPCA center is 3 km north of the town of Santa Clara, Pastaza, and 10 km south of the town of Carlos Julio Arosemena Tola, Napo province.  The CIPCA property includes 2848 hectares of which about 2000 hectares are primary forest at 600-1100 m elevation near the base of the Andes, and frontage along the Anzu and Piatua rivers.   The herbarium includes collections made in Ecuador since 1985, as well  as recent collections since 2012 by herbarium staff and collaborators.

The ECUAMZ herbarium is normally open to visitor Monday-Friday, 8:30 to 16:30, but is closed at present due to the virus pandemic (June 2020)



on the outskirts of Puyo, Pastaza.  In mid-2013, the herbarium will move to permanent quarters at the University`s research station, the ""Centro de Investigación Postgrado y Conservación Amazónica"

DSUM has been transferred to BHSC.   The Dakota State University Herbarium  was originally housed in a small rural university in south central South Dakota.  The collection  focused on plants collected regionally in the glacial prairie-pothole lake region of transition tall grass-short grass prairie of the Northern Great Plains  In addition to serving as a resource for teaching, the herbarium was a temporal and spatial repository of plants collected periodically during the rapid conversion of native prairie to cropland during the 20th Century.  This conversion accelerated during the century and continues today.  A very small diminishing fraction of native prairie remains.  Because of the regional emphasis of the collections, the  herbarium served as a resource to allow research on species composition and distribution regionally as affected by global warming and global climate change.

The Hoyt Arboretum Herbarium’s primary focus is to document and verify the arboretum’s internationally-renowned living tree collection, which currently has over 2,500 species. We aim to voucher every species in our living collection, adding approximately 300 to 500 herbarium sheets per year. Additionally, HAH functions as a reference library for City of Portland staff and partners, especially in the identification of regionally significant invasive weeds and street trees. 
 
Herbarium specimens and our living tree collection can be remotely accessed through  our online plant inventory (https://hoytarboretum.gardenexplorer.org/) and we are working to get our specimen data and images available online through the regional Consortium of Pacific Northwest Herbaria (https://www.pnwherbaria.org/).

data.notes: In Uzbekistan, rich herbarium collections of extant plants as well as a valuable palaeobotanical collection have been gathered since the first herbarium of this region was founded in 1920. Prior to 1988, these collections were housed at the Tashkent State University (TAK), the Tashkent Pedagogic Institute, the Nature Museum of Uzbekistan (RNMUT), the former Samarkand State University, and the Institutes of Botany (TASH), of Microbiology (TASM), and of Chemistry of Plant Materials, belonging to the Academy of Sciences of the Republic Uzbekistan. In 1988 these herbaria were combined as the Central Herbarium of the Academy of Sciences of the Republic Uzbekistan and housed at the Botanical Institute. The acronym T ASH is to be used for the Central Herbarium.

Entered Feb 2014. The herbarium moved from Johannesburg to Nelspruit area during 1998. The herbarium building, which  incorporates the  library and an annex for mounting and freezing of specimens at Whyte Thorne, was inaugurated in Feb 2001. The herbarium has been privately owned and funded from inception in 1967. The Herbarium, Library and Garden are open to all bona-fide botanically motivated persons. Whyte Thorne Botanic Garden has been developed on the same property, consisting  of 23 hectares of which six acres comprise the laid –out garden and nursery including a 900sq m shade house & 34sq m propagation house. WTBG is a privately sponsored botanic Garden with 8300 living plant accessions, 6500 living plant orchid accessions and 11990 seed accessions. Accession numbers are cross-referenced to herbarium material where appropriate.
D. McMurtry collecting numbers currently stand at 15200 of which ±7500 pressed specimens are lodged at the Johannesburg Botanic Garden Herbarium, the rest in HSMC. Duplicates in PRE and BNRH. Specimens mostly from the four northern provinces of S.Af. but include Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Namibia, Tanzania, Kenya, St Helena, Reunion, Madagascar and Comores . Carpological Spirit material (mostly Orchidaceae) collections maintained.

The vascular plant collections (a total of about 300 000 specimens) are mainly from the territory of Poland (99%), foreign collections (1%) are represented mainly by plants from North Africa and America. The oldest foreign collections are from the 19th century (collectors: T.R.J. Nitschke, E. Bourgeau, R.F. Hohenacker T. Kotschy, A.G. von Schrenk, G. Lorinser and others).The oldest national collections are from 1920s and 1930s  from Lodz and Tatra MTs. (M. Potęga) and from the vicinity of Vilno (now Lithuania, J.Steckiewicz).
The liverworts collections (a total of more than 1626) are mainly from Central Poland. This collection includes also specimens from Hepaticotheca Polonica (J. Szweykowski, T. Wojterska, S. Updated 3 Mar 2022, from Sergei Mosyakin, Kyiv: The Karazin University of Kharkiv is located in a complex of huge buildings near the Freedom Square (Ploshcha Svobody), the largest city square in Europe, Bombing of this area has partly destroyed or severly damaged those buildings.

The section with the CWU herbarium was also damaged, but not so badly; there and no windows in the herbarium premises anymore, but herbarium staff people came without hesitation to the place after the airstrikes and tried to cover the frames with cardboard and plywood. As far as I know, at present there is no loss of specimens, but under the current wet weather conditions the specimens are in fact open to the elements.            


Update from Oct 2020.  The name of the University was changed from Kharkiv State University to V. N. Karazin National University. CWU consists of three parts: 1) Kharkiv Botanical Garden (former CWB, now part of CWU); 2) Department of Botany; 3) Department of Mycology and Plant Resistance - CWU (Myc). (curator O.Yu. Akulov)

Information about the Mycological Herbarium
Dr. Olexander Akulov, curator of the Mycological Herbarium CWU-Myc (V.N. Karazin National University of Kharkiv, Ukraine) addresses you. I am very grateful to you for your kind letter of support and suggestions for help. This is very important for us.
 
I apologize for being late in replying to your letter. In the conditions of hostilities, it is difficult for me to answer letters in time. 
 
CWU-Myc – the oldest and second-largest collection of herbarised fungi in Ukraine, that has the status of the National Heritage of Ukraine. It holds about 40,000 specimens, including a large collection of old mycological exsiccates. There are many type specimens and memorial collections of world-famous scientists among them. The oldest specimen in our collection dates back to 1797. In modern times the collection is being intensively replenished with new materials. Some of them represent species that are new to science, including new genera.
 
Our herbarium has already survived several wars of the past. During WW2, part of the collection was not evacuated. It was placed in metal boxes and buried in the ground in the botanical garden, where it lay for several years. After the war, part of the collection that was evacuated never returned to Kharkiv. It was moved to Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine, and still, it is housed in the KW herbarium. That part, which was buried underground, is still stored in CWU. 
 
The current war with Russia has caused enormous damage to the city of Kharkiv and the University in particular. In the large city with about 1.5 million citizens, about 20% of homes were destroyed, including several buildings of the University.
 
Fortunately, the herbarium has survived till now. The blast shattered the windows, but we closed them from rain and wind with plywood and polyethylene. The samples are stored in airtight metal boxes and are reasonably well protected. This will not protect the collection from a cruise missile or air bomb, but we will hope for the best. Now the Ukrainian army has pushed the invaders 40 km away from the city, so the shelling has decreased to some level.
 
None of us could have imagined that the horrors of war would be repeated in central Europe in the 21st century. We were not ready for such a situation. And the current force majeure has very clearly shown what we did right and where we made mistakes. 
 
As never before, we are aware of the importance of digitizing our funds. We were moving in that direction, but not fast enough. The University already has the status of Data publisher in GBIF. In collaboration with the University of Tartu via PlutoF platform, we have digitized about 7,000 samples. Information about 6,000 of them is already available to anyone in the world through the GBIF site. In 2021, we have prepared information for about another 2,000 specimens.
 
From the first days of the war, the main server of the University stopped working, and with it stopped the access to the electronic archive and catalog of the herbarium disappeared. Only due to the fact that Dr. O. Prylutskyi had a backup copy of the data and posted it on a server in Norway, access to the information was restored.
 
In 2021, we also started a revision of valuable specimens from the CWU-Myc herbarium using molecular genetic markers. We already obtained about 200 sequences. As a result of this work we are preparing a series of publications, for example, https://ukrbotj.co.ua/archive/79/2/84  Unfortunately, about 300 amplicons and all reagents for molecular research were lost during the war, and it will not be easy to restore them.

Description of the fungarium or fungal specimen:
The BIOTEC Fungal Herbarium was established in 1996 and registered with Index Herbariorum in 2003. The herbarium has resided in a purpose-built, climate- and humidity-controlled facility since 2003. BBH has been ISO9001-certified for quality management since 2004. There are over 100 species of type specimens in the containers. Nearly half of the greater than 49,000 specimens are insect pathogenic fungi. Other significant groups include macrofungi collected in Thailand from diverse Basidiomycota and Ascomycota phyla. In 2019, the repository changed its official name from BIOTEC to National Biobank of Thailand (NBT), but it remains under the National Science and Technology Development Agency (NSTDA). The location has been relocated from the Storage Building to the Innovation Crustor II Tower A, 1st Floor, but remains within the same region of Thailand Science Park in Pathum Thani Province.

Description of the plant herbarium:
The BIOTEC Plant Herbarium is managed by the Ecology and Geo-informatics Lab, and specializes in storing and distributing voucher specimens from the biodiversity research plots established by the Lab. Its main plot is the 30-ha forest dynamics plot in Khao Yai National Park. Voucher specimens from other research projects within BIOTEC and outside collaborators are also stored.

data.notes: The Herbarium Hyderabadensis (HY), being established in the year 1930, is housed at the Department of Botany, Osmania University, Hyderabad, Telangana state, India.  It holds approximately 8000 specimens, collected from all around the world. The Herbarium Hyderabadensis (HY) derives its name from the existing locale called Hyderabad, Deccan. It was recognised as one of Asian and international Herbaria (Index Herbariorum: http://sweetgum.nybg.org/science/ih/herbarium-details/?irn=125627). The collections are maintained under high quality standards for its standing. As it is in vogue for Indian (Commonwealth) herbaria, the specimens are arranged as per the system of classification of Bentham & Hooker (1862‒1883). The re-arrangement of specimens as per LAPG (2009) and APG IV is on the way.  The Accession Register of HY includes the name of the plant, plant collector and the date of collection, habitat (nation, state/region, district, place, etc. HY has successfully documented the flora of the erstwhile state of Andhra Pradesh (now it is segregated into Andhra Pradesh and Telangana in 2014). The specimens at HY enable one for preparing/developing interactive identifications key for the Angiosperms of the two states (habitat-wise) and as per growth forms (trees, shrubs, climbers and herbs). The herbarium collections are added actively at the rate of 500‒1000 specimens per year on the average.

data.notes:
PSUB primarily houses the legacy collection of Peter A. Smith who lived and worked in and around the Okavango Delta for more than 30 years.
In 2022 we have returned to preparing specimen sheets for digital scanning. We are prioritizing the core, legacy, collection.
During 2021 we focused on preparing specimen sheets of those species used as Traditional Medicinal Plants in Botswana and particularly those used for the treatment of respiratory symptoms as seen in Covid19 infection. These herbarium sheets have been digital scanned and we will enter data from the image into our database (BRAHMS).
Visitors with specialist botanical knowledge would be welcome to assist with determination of specimens from various families. Expertise in Poaceae or Cyperaceae would be of particular benefit to us.

data.notes: Entered Aug 2016 (new curator).  The UST Museum of Arts and Sciences was founded by a professor of Natural History, Fr. Ramon Martinez Vigil, O.P. in 1870 at Intramuros, Manila. With the efforts of Fr. Casto de Elera O.P.,  the  natural sciences collections were scientifically classified and catalogued. Before World War II, the UST Museum of Arts and Sciences was transferred to its present site, at the UST Main Bldg., Sampaloc, Manila. In 1988, a large part of the plant collection composed of 8 herbarium cases of about 8,200 specimens were transferred to the Research Center for the Natural Sciences at the 4th floor, Clinical Division of the UST Hospital. Since then, the UST Herbarium is continuously being replenished with new specimens through the collections made by the UST RCNS research team, graduate and undergraduate students. With the completion of the Thomas Aquinas Research Complex in November 2001, the plant collections were moved to its new and modern location.  The herbarium is equipped with modern facilities and an adjacent laboratory for herbarium curation.

It aims to be a resource for biological systematics and classification, diversity and conservation, biotechnological applications, biological monitoring, biodeterioration, bioremediation, climate change, ecology, and pharmaceutical bio-prospecting. The Biotechnology department was established in 1980, and has 22 scientific members from different disciplines of biotechnology, microbiology, mycology and lichenology. The Iranian Research Organization for Science and Technology (IROST) is a governmental organization, founded in 1980, with the aim of providing support to Iranian researchers, inventors and industrialists across the country. This organization provides valuable services in fulfilling the country\'s scientific, technical and engineering requirements through supporting applied and developmental research as well as developing new technologies by exploiting qualified experts and modern equipment and facilities.

data.associatedHerbaria: Yugra State University
data.notes:
The YSU BC currently stores about 15000 specimens of fungi, mosses, hepatics and vascular plants. It was initially based on private collections of several researchers working on biodiversity assessment in Yugra State University. In 2017 YSU BC is registered as a data publisher in GBIF (https://www.gbif.org/publisher/fa46e267-4d25-41f5-bbbe-1cd75860b943).
The main goal of the YSU BC is to develop reference library of regional biodiversity, support research in systematics, ecology, phylogeny and applied disciplines, and manage associated biodiversity information in the Northern West Siberia. For that purpose, we are developing conditions for physical storage of samples, facilitating their scientific analysis, and applying modern computer technologies for storage, analysis and distribution of collection data.
The database of YSU BC is developed using Specify software. The Specify Web Portal (http://bioportal.ugrasu.ru/) available for the database search, browsing the map and images, and download. The database is shared through GBIF by IPT software using MySQL queries to each individual collection, including images of specimens.
Published papers about the collection:

Filippova NV, Filippov IV, Lapshina ED (2020) Establishing the regional center on biodiversity data mobilization in the Northwestern Siberia (Russia). ARPHA Proceedings 2: 27-35. https://doi.org/10.3897/ap.2.e58693

contact.phone: Northwestern University Ecological Park & Botanic Gardens

data.associatedHerbaria: Northwestern University and Ecotourism Park and Botanical Garden(BGCI).  Other sites:  covering 5 national park of Region 1, Philippines
data.notes:
The Northwestern University in the Philippines is a pioneering academic institution in the Northern Luzon geared in conserving the natural heritage of the country. The northwestern Luzon is home to numerous endemic plants species and cannot be found elsewhere in the world, despite is harsh climatic condition, natural calamities and human exploitation that aggravated the degradation of natural plant habitats. The Philippines is among the Megadiversity countries in the world yet among the most critically endangered, placing it as a hotspot for conservation. The university established its botanic gardens to perform the international agenda of botanic gardens in conservation and to halt the loss of species in our region.

The herbarium Includes 2,200 species of living plant collections at the Systematic Gardens with 226 Families and 124 subfamilies of the kingdom Plantae. The living plant collection and herbarium collections are extensively used for plant taxonomy (APG III). Top universities in Manila (University of the Philippines Diliman, University of the Philippines Manila, University of Santo Tomas and the De La Salle University Dasmarinas Cavite) annually conduct taxonomy courses in the botanic gardens which is arranged according to family and in their latest phylogenetic treatment

The specimens are also sent to the different botanical institutions around the world for DNA barcoding and genomics.

All specimens are newly acquired and collected in the wild to represent Flora of the Island Luzon, Philippines.

data.notes: Updated Oct 2023. ECWP herbarium is open to any researcher and amateur, by appointment, on request. However validation by the ECWP Operation Director is mandatory. The ECWP herbarium is located at ECWP headquarters in Missour, Morocco, in a building dedicated to botanical studies. Specimens are mounted on acid-free, archival paper (48 x 28 cm) and are stored in cardboard boxes, that are themselves in cabinets. 2450 Moroccan taxa are currently in the collection, including some types specimens.  Many vouchers have been verified by Mohammed Ibn Tattou (Institut Scientifique de Rabat), one of the authors of the Flore pratique du Maroc. There is an Excel file list of identified specimens vouchers. A software dedicated to sample collection management is planned for 2024. ECWP also has a botanical bibliographical collection, specializing in south-west Mediterranean flora and habitats, that includes 400 books and monographs and >10000 pdf files (books, monographs, papers). There is a flora/fauna database in the production for over fifteen years, including over 1500 recent phytosociological relevés.

data.notes: Updated March 10 2022:  Our collection LWS has over 118K herbarium vouchers collected during the last 200 years. This collection has crucial importance because it hosts many specimens from the Carpathian region. We evacuated type specimens from our herbarium. But, unfortunately, we were unable to relocate the whole herbarium collection due to lack of space and finances. Our herbarium is deposited in metallic boxes that can resist mechanical damage and more or less to the water and humidity. However, these boxes are not temperature-resistant and therefore there is a high risk of smoldering of herbarium specimens inside these boxes in case of fire and high temperatures. It would be great to cover these boxes by fire-resistant thermo-isolation (e.g., by Rockwool RockSlab) to prevent the thermal damage of specimens for the period of war, but we have no such financial possibilities.The collection includes the former Herbarium of Shevchenko's Scientific Society

data.notes: The HERBARIO UNIVERSITARIO PORT  (INBIO-UNELLEZ) has a collection of about 150,000 botanical specimens of vascular plants. The collection is organized in alphabetical order by three main collections: Pteridophytes, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms (PPG and APG system). Herbarium PORT also contains the most modern and representative national vascular plants of the Guayana, Amazon and lowland forests and savannas of Western Llanos of Venezuela. Also, it holds the most comprehensive collection of Pteridophytes of Venezuela, as well as, important collections from the Andean foothills and Guaramacal National Park in the Venezuelan Andes. Herbarium PORT also has a collection of types of Neotropical vascular plants of approximately 500 specimens. The types specimens held by PORT are 70 Holotypes, 110 Isotypes, 280 Paratypes among other ca. 40 type specimens non-specified yet. These type specimens represent ca. 250 species, belonging to 138 genera and 64 families of vascular plants.

The herbarium was established from 1974 when Murdoch University opened, principally to support ecological research and teaching. Situated on the lands of the Whadjuk people, the boodjar (country) of the Murdoch campus has, for thousands of years, been a place of learning. We at Murdoch University are proud to continue this long tradition. Most specimens in the herbarium are from the Southwest, Darling Plateau, Eneabba, Fitzgerald River National Park, and Pilbara regions of Western Australia. Significant sets are from the Murdoch University campus (which retains several areas of native vegetation), bushland remnants around the City of Melville, riverine habitats along the Swan and Canning Rivers, and an area of Queens Park that is now covered with houses. data.notes: Updated Feb 2023.  The Herbarium of the Arkansas Natural Heritage Commission consists primarily of specimens collected in the course of statewide ecological and biological inventory work conducted by the Arkansas Natural Heritage Program.  Many of the specimens represent species that are rare in the state or were collected from rare or unusual habitats.  The goals of the collection are 1) to provide a reference collection for work performed by Natural Heritage Commission staff and their conservation partners, 2) to house voucher specimens for rare plant records in the database of the Arkansas Natural Heritage Program, and 3) to voucher plants of ecologically sensitive or otherwise significant lands, including those contained within the State's System of Natural Areas.  While most specimens are from Arkansas, special care is being made to assemble a collection of plants from surrounding states that are not presently known in Arkansas but are likely to be found there.  The herbarium has new custom-built housing, with accompanying lab and research rooms,  Compactor units were installed in late 2016.

data.notes: We are pleased to announce the donation of the College of Santa Fe Herbarium to the UNM Herbarium in the Museum of Southwestern Biology, University of New Mexico.    The collection includes over 1800 specimens of vascular plants and several hundred bryophytes, hepatics, and lichens, largely collected by Brother Arsène Brouard in the 1920's and 30's in New Mexico. Brother Arsène was the first collector to work extensively in northern New Mexico since the early botanical explorations in the 1840s by Gambel, Wislizenus, Emory, and Fendler.  Wooten and Standley collected east of Santa Fe briefly in 1908.  Arsène’s notes indicate that he collected at least 5,000 specimens in northern New Mexico, several thousand of which are at the Smithsonian and nearly 1800 are in the donated herbarium from The College of Santa Fe.  There are also a number of specimens collected in Mexico by Brother Arsène.  The specimens will not be available for study until they are curated and databased.

importantCollectors: A. de F. Gomes e Sousa
data.notes: Updated Jan 2010.  Since 1879 the Herbarium of the Department of Botany of the University of Coimbra, Portugal (COI), has owned the Herbarium of the german (Saxonian) Henrich Moritz Willkomm, Professor at Prague University and a specialist on the flora of the Iberian Peninsula. This collection was bought to Willkomm and contains vascular and non-vascular plants of the Mediterranean area and the Macaronesian Islands and includes c. 10.000 species and over 30.000 specimens. The specimens were collected by Willkomm himself and other relevant botanical collectors of the time e.g., Bourgeau, Orphanides, Sieber, Lange, Loscos, Boissier, Reuter, Lagasca, Cavanilles. It was the basis for Willkomm & Lange's Prodromus Florae Hispanicae (1861-1880), the first comprehensive Flora of most of the Iberian Peninsula - only now being superseded by the Flora iberica (Castroviejo et al., 1986-, Madrid) - and contains many type specimens of Iberian taxa. Not all Willkomm specimens are at COI and some are scattered in other institutes. But this is by far the largest assemblage of his material and he regarded it as his core collection which, as a whole he sold to Júlio Henriques, the founder of COI. data.notes: Entered Dec 2017. The Herbarium SLUI has a collection of plants that have been collected since 1988 in the State of Maranhão. Since 2009, the Herbarium has been registered in the Brazilian Herbarium Network of the Brazilian Botanic Society (SBB) as Herbarium Rosa Mochel (SLUI), and in 2010 it joined the INCT - Virtual Herbarium Institute of Flora and Fungi of Brazil. With the support of INCT - Virtual Herbarium of Flora and Fungi of Brazil and FAPEMA, SLUI began the process of computerizing the data of the collection, and its inclusion in the speciesLink network, of the Reference Center on Environmental Information. In 2017 the scanning of the collection with image capture began. Currently 131 exsicatas (about 2% of the collection) are available online on the speciesLink network. The SLUI collection has about 5,500 samples of botanical material, mainly exsicates, predominating the angiosperms, with 117 families represented. The collection also has 50 pteridophytes, 26 bryophytes, 24 macroscopic algae and two gymnosperms. In addition to the collection of exsicatas, a xiloteca (174 specimens), a carpoteca (50 specimens), a collection of seeds (35 samples) and a small collection of macroscopic fungi (10 samples) are available. The collections represent mainly the vegetation of the state: Amazonian forest; Thick; The majority of samples come from the State of Maranhão (70%), although there is a collection of flora from 15 states in Brazil, mainly from donations. The main families represented are Fabaceae (616 records), Malvaceae (420), Cyperaceae (340), Malpighiaceae (290) and Asteraceae (270).

data.associatedHerbaria: University of Washington
data.notes:
The UW Bothell Herbarium provides a critical authoritative record of plants occurring in the University of Washington Bothell and Cascadia College co-located campus wetland and the greater North Creek Basin. As the vegetation changes through time in the wetland it will form a reliable record to help us and future researchers understand biological and habitat change in one of our regions’ preeminent floodplain restoration projects. Collections focus on Snohomish and north King Counties, Washington, USA. It functions primarily as a teaching collection for undergraduate students, faculty, and researchers. It is open to the public by appointment.

The herbarium was founded in 2009 by Tyson Kemper, and 150 collections were added over the course of 7 years. In 2015, Sarah Verlinde started collecting as a student researcher. While collecting, she started a small volunteer team, and in the first year added another 100 specimens. In 2016, Sarah was hired full-time by the Office of Research (the herbarium sponsor), and continued to run the herbarium on a part-time basis. In three years, her team has added 750 more specimens. They joined an online consortium through the University of Washington herbarium at the Burke Museum (WTU) and now photograph and publish the specimens online at www.pnwherbaria.org.

incorporatedHerbaria: BIF-CEYL (Herbier de Ceylan collected by Hermann; Ms 973 Res, 213 specimens on 171 pages)
BIF-LAPP (Herbier de Laponie collected by Linnaeus; Ms 3912 Res, 379 specimens on 155 pages)
data.notes: The library of the Institut de France in Paris holds two important herbaria bound in separate folio volumes. They were originally part of the collection of Johannes Burman (1706-1779) and his son Nicolaas Laurens Burman (1734-1793) which was acquired by Benjamin Delessert (1773-1847) in 1801 (see Wijnands et al., 2017). Delessert’s herbarium came to the City of Geneva in 1869 while his library went to the Institut de France. The main Burman herbarium is now incorporated in the Pre-Linnaean herbarium in Geneva (now G-PREL). However, two bound herbarium volumes were treated as part of the Delessert manuscripts and given to the Institut de France. The first of these contains material from Ceylon collected by Paul Hermann (1646-1695) which was the main basis of Johannes Burman’s Thesaurus Zeylanicus. Lourteig (1966) has provided a detailed catalogue of this herbarium (now BIF-CEYL). The second herbarium volume contains material collected by Carl Linnæus (1707-1778) during his Lapland journey in 1732. data.notes:
The Department of Botany is one of the oldest departments in the University, being established in 1912.  Prof. Shiv Ram Kashyap, who was the department head from 1912 to 1934, established a museum and herbarium. The herbarium’s holdings included plants from many regions, including China, Indonesia and Philippines, and its collection of liverworts and mosses was considered the largest in the subcontinent at that time. The collection grew to include several hundred specimens of algae, fungi, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms but, when the University of the Punjab was established as a separate institution, most of the specimens were transferred there. The present museum and herbarium are named the Prof. Kashyap Museum and Dr. Sultan Ahmed Herbarium. Both are being actively developed. 

The Department also has a botanic garden, Botanic Garden GCU, which was founded in 1912 and extends over 7 acres. It has long been recognized for the diversity of its holdings. It is home to Pakistan’s Botanic Gardens Network Secretariat.

In addition the collection contains over several hundred specimens of microalgae (including the blue algae) on microscope slides. The most valuable exsiccata from the 19th and early 20th century are associated in the collections of L. Rabenhorst (collected in the years 1848-1877). data.notes:
The J.J. Triana Herbarium (HJJT) promotes the floristic knowledge of the mountainous regions of Colombia and northern South America, contributing to the sustainable appropriation of natural resources, the ecological restoration of mountain ecosystems, and their conservation over time, in a joint effort among academia, civil society and rural communities.

The HJJT Herbarium is a repository of dried botanical specimens of angiosperms, gymnosperms, ferns and lycophytes, bryophytes, lichens and macro fungi. It also considers the preservation of ancillary samples of seeds and fruits, material in liquid preservative, tissues in silica gel, and prepared microscope slides. The collection also houses a Spore and Tissue Bank of Isoetes and Pteridophyta, dried and preserved in Eppendorf tubes.

Its mission is to encourage research and knowledge construction on Colombian and Neotropical flora, with emphasis on high and middle mountain ecosystems, providing strategic floristic and environmental data as supplies for accurate environmental decisions, as well as to plan and implement strategic actions towards the conservation and sustainable use of renewable natural resources at local, national and regional scales.
