Entered Jan 2020.
Qarshi Botanical Garden,  is located on the premises of Qarshi Industries (Pvt.) Ltd, Industrial Estate Hattar, District Haripur, KPK, Pakistan on Taxila - Haripur road. It is 60 km from zero-point Islamabad. The geographical significance of Haripur district lies in the fact that its boundaries touch Abbotabad in north-east, Margalla hills of Islamabad in the South-east, Swat valley in the north-west and Sawabi district in the west. Besides, two districts of Punjab province i.e. Attock &Rawalpindi lie on the south-west & south-east respectively. Hattar Industrial Estate, Haripur falls under sub-tropical climatic zone and is situated in the foothills of Himalayas at the latitude 33º 44' to 34º 22' and longitude 72 º 35' to 73º 15' and 610 m above sea level. The mean minimum & maximum annual rainfall ranges from 800 - 1300 mm respectively & average winter temperature is 12oC and summer temperature is around 29oC. However, maximum temperature rises to >40ºC in summer and the lowest temperature in the winter fall below - 4ºC. Depending upon the weather conditions, sometime severe frost is observed during the month of December & January.
Medicinal plant species are those that provide people with medicines to prevent diseases, maintain health or cure ailment. Therefore, medicinal plants are important in the wellbeing of people yet most people are not aware about these species or their medicinal value. Examples of these plants include Aloe vera, Azadirachta indica and many others.
Medicinal plant species are of great value to mankind and other animals but not much emphasis is laid on their conservation, especially ex-situ conservation, given their ever dwindling natural habitats. Conservation of medicinal plants involves the sustainable utilization of medicinal plant resources that is in such a way that they satisfy the needs of today’s generation without hindering the ability of tomorrow’s generations to satisfy their own needs. This can easily be simplified as: “when you are eating today, remember to leave some for those who will be there tomorrow.”
Some of the plant species have already been extinct, other are declared threatened, endangered or rare mainly due to improper harvesting practices incompatible with their survival or habitat degradation due to landuse changes in favor of the development paradigm. The ever-dwindling natural habitats of these medicinal plants have left ex-situ conservation as the most preferable choice. This ex-situ conservation falls under the programs of institutions such as botanic gardens/herbal gardens that are encouraged by the Convention on Biological Diversity framework.
Therefore, Qarshi Industries (Pvt) Ltd. under its environmental policy and biodiversity conservation agenda has committed itself to protect, conserve and propagate endangered plant species in general and medicinal plant species in particular. To achieve the objectives, Qarshi Botanical Garden (QBG) was established in 2001 to conserve and propagate commercially important indigenous plant species.

data.notes: Entered Май 2020. Founded in 1912, Herbarium of the Vologda State University aims to study the phytodiversity of the Vologda Region. During its existence, the herbarium was located in the city of Vologda; still, it repeatedly changed its formal affiliations: Vologda Teachers Training Institute (1912–1918), Vologda Pedagogical Institute (1918–1923), Severnyi Krai Pedagogical Institute (1930–1932), Vologda State Pedagogical Institute (1932–1995), Vologda State Pedagogical University (1995–2014), and Vologda State University (2014–to date). For the last thirty years, the herbarium has a dual purpose and is used for educational and scientific purposes. For ease of use, it is divided into three sections: main, geographic, and demonstration sections. The main section includes collections of higher vascular plants and cryptogams (bryophytes and lichens). These collections mainly cover the Vologda Region, yet with high density. The main section comprises samples from at least 250 local floras. Herbarium possesses one isotype and two paratypes of Potamogeton × vepsicus. A number of specimens were reviewed by specialists in complex taxonomic groups: P. Uotila (Chenopodiaceae), A.N. Sennikov (Cotoneaster), A.A. Bobrov (Potamogetonaceae, Batrachium, Myriophyllum), V.G. Papchenkov (Salix, Typha). The collection of bryophytes was partially reviewed by E.A. Ignatova. The geographic section of the herbarium contains specimens from the herbaria of botanical gardens (BAK, CHIS, VBGI, Batumi, Sukhumi), universities (LECB, AR, PSK, RV, SIMF, URP, Samarkand State University, Turkmen State Pedagogical Institut

data.organization: Fort Worth Nature Center and Refuge
data.notes: Entered Febf. 2020.  At 3,621 acres, the Fort Worth Nature Center and Refuge is one of the largest city-owned nature centers in the United States.  Created in the 1960s with the help of local citizens’ groups, the Center’s development built on earlier efforts to protect the watershed feeding the Lake Worth reservoir in the western portion of the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex.  Dora Sylvester, a science educator and naturalist who was a major force in the Center’s creation, understood the importance of herbaria in documenting past and present plant diversity at managed nature preserves, and established the FWNC herbarium.  The herbarium started mainly with her own collections from the property and has been supplemented with vouchers from more recent vegetation studies, as well as those made by other volunteers, staff, and students from local universities.  The herbarium additionally serves a role in the training of staff and volunteers, and also in the Center’s education programs for adults and school children.

data.notes: Entered May 2021.  The St. Edward’s University Herbarium, which was established in the late 1950s, is a fruit of the work of Brother Daniel Lynch, CSC, and his dedicated students. Br. Daniel (1921–1997) was beloved throughout Central Texas, and many university benefactors contributed to funds that supported his scholarship and his service to marginalized communities. He used some of those funds to buy herbarium cabinets and supplies as he built the collection. He relied heavily on the herbarium as he worked with the illustrator, Nancy McGowan, to complete ""Native and Naturalized Woody Plants of Austin and the Hill Country."" This reference was originally published in 1981 and is still widely used by botanists around the state. In addition to his high level of scholarship, Br. Daniel was a stellar teacher at St. Edward’s for more than 40 years. His students not only learned from the herbarium collection, but they also helped him to build it. Today, the collection is used primarily to support teaching in the natural sciences, but also serves as a repository for voucher specimens documenting the plant diversity of the associated Wild Basin Wilderness Preserve and Creative Research Center.

data.organization: Oblastní muzeum a galerie v Mostě
data.geography: Czech Republic, especially Northwestern Bohemia (marginally also other parts of Central Europe)
data.notes:
Entered May 2021. The main part of the herbarium of The Regional Museum and Gallery in Most town is the collection of 1352 specimens created by Jaromír Sládek. It is dated since 1981 to 1992, and it mainly contains records of halophilous and thermophilous taxa from the Northwestern Bohemia (Czech Republic). 
Another part of the collection was created by Bedřich Hulán. It contains about 850 herbarium specimens recording vascular plants flora of northern part of the Most county (i.e. Litvínov town and its vicinity) in years 1950–1961. Another two historical collections created by Anton Roth and Anton Nowák originated in 19th century. Both are of great regional importance owing to including many specimens from totally destroyed localities due to long-term coal mining and another large landscape changes in the region of Northwestern Bohemia.
Current herbarium accessories are focused on document of vascular plant taxa including woody plants and also taxonomically problematic species in the northwestern Bohemia and adjacent regions. The herbarium is currently systematically enriched with vascular plant taxa which has not been included in the collection yet.

data.notes:
Our collection of plants constitutes a Medicinal Ethnobotanical Herbarium, since the North of Argentina is a privileged area, not only due to the tradition of use of plant species in vernacular medicine, but also due to the extensive existing documentation regarding the use of plants by the aborigines in natural medicine, among which are the tribes (MOCOVÍ, WICHÍ, TOBA). That is why the systematization of the practices that revolve around the recovery of the use of medicinal plants began, where botanical, ecological and anthropological knowledge converge with a scientific basis of the connections that exist between cultural groups and their plant environment.
The main functions of the \""Carlos Chifa\"" herbarium are:
Entered June 2021.
 
This Herbarium, which the “Universidad nacional del Chaco Austral” proudly owns, was the imprint of the Agronomist Carlos Chifa back in 1994, being at that time the Facultad de Agroindustria belonging to UNNE (Universidad Nacional del Nordeste), who making use of his knowledge in the Botanical field and creating strong ties with the original peoples of the region, he knew how to create a large collection of medicinal plants, with more than 5,000 specimens. Serving not only as a source of information for the careers of Medicine, Pharmacy, Veterinary Medicine and Zootechnical Engineering, but also for scientific studies that have been carried out in our house of higher studies.
This information resulted in the Publication of 4 books, which are:
_ Chifa, C. y Ricciardi, A. I. A. (2001). Plantas de uso en medicina vernácula del centro del Chaco argentino. Fundación Miguel Lillo.
_ Chifa, C. (2005). Plantas medicinales usadas por las comunidades aborígenes del Chaco argentino. Editorial Universitaria de la Universidad Nacional del Nordeste.
_ Chifa, C. y Ricciardi A. I. A. (2011). Plantas medicinales usadas por las comunidades aborígenes del Chaco argentino (2 ed.) Ediciones Elemento.
_ Chifa, C. y Ricciardi A. I. A. (2014). Las plantas medicinales del nordeste argentino en las crónicas de la época de la Colonia. Ediciones Elemento.

data.notes:
Entered Feb 2022.  Established in 1961, the Louisiana State Arboretum was the first such area in the South and the first state-supported arboretum in the United States. The 600 acre site is the only Louisiana state-owned  preservation area open to the public, providing a little over 5.5 miles of hiking trails along a Cypress-Tupelo Swamp, through a Bottomland Hardwood Forest and along ridges of a Beech-Magnolia Forest. 
In 1967, Horticulturist Nick A. Tuzzalino collected some of the first plants to be preserved for the arboretum’s herbarium.  In the early 1980’s, Charles A. Allen, at that time a Botany graduate student, was hired to collect and preserve as many plant specimens as he could find and identify in the initial 300 acres open to the public.  There are now about 600 specimens in the herbarium collection.

Entered Jun 2022.  Our herbarium started in 2011 belonging to the Laboratory of Palynostratigraphy and Paleobotany (di Pasquo and Silvestri, 2014), in the Center for Scientific Research and technology transfer to production CICYTTP (CONICET-ER-UADER), sited in Diamante, Entre Ríos province, Argentina.
It is composed of plants collected mainly in the El Palmar National Park located in the eastern Entre Ríos Province where the palm Butia yatay is the main protected tree of a savanna environment along with Poaceae and Asteraceae (see Batista et al. 2014; Rodriguez et al. 2017). di Pasquo et al. (2016) published for the first time, in situ spores using the Herbarium Lorentz (code DTE), which belongs to the CICYTTP. A new herbarium collection is registered herein with the acronym LPPH to include spores and pollen in situ mostly from Entre Ríos but also, from other regions of Argentina. The LPP is also registered as colaborator group of the RCPol - Red de Catálogos Polínicos online (http://rcpol.org.br/es/quem-somos/labs-grupos-pesquisa/laboratorio-de-palinoestratigrafia-y-paleobotanica/) since 2016.
The specimens are not digitalized yet, although they are given a number in a spreadsheet.

data.notes: Entered Sep 2022.  Our herbarium houses all ranks of plants families ranging from Bryophytes, Lycophytes, Ferns and Fern allies, Gymnosperms, Basal Angiosperms, Magnoliids, Eudicot and Monocots of Perak phytogeographical province and its sub province. This area actually rich in endemic plants due to the overlapping of three different forests i.e. the Asiatic seasonal intrusion, limestone hills and the main range forests. The Perak phytogeographical areas is known as special pocket of endemic plants. On top of that, Perak also has a coastal hill dipterocarp forest, that is unique to our world. The Royal Belum of the northern of Perak is known as the oldest forest that still not fully surveyed. Our voucher specimen collections covers all areas of Perak phytogeographical region.

data.associatedHerbaria: State Herbarium of South Australia (AD)
data.notes:
Entered Oct 2022.  The Terrestrial Ecosystem Research Network (TERN) is Australia’s land ecosystem observatory and is enabled by the Australian Government’s National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS). 

TERN measures key terrestrial ecosystem attributes over time from continental scale to fields sites at hundreds of representative locations across Australia’s major biomes and openly provide model ready data that enable researchers to detect and interpret changes in land ecosystems. 

TERN’s Ecosystem Surveillance platform conducts field surveys and sampling across a national network of plots and transects to provide the data, samples and advice required for improved monitoring and assessment of Australia’s major ecosystem. The platform helps scientists and land managers better detect and quantify change in vegetation structure and composition, land cover and soil characteristics. 
The platform collects representative plant specimens within the 1ha plots and associated leaf tissue samples stored in Silica Gel. The specimens are thus part of a long-term continental scale ecological monitoring program with rich temporal data. Plant specimens are collected on each revisit; therefore, the collection differs to that of a traditional herbarium. The plant specimen collection represents 5,804 vascular plant species, equating to 24.18% of the Australian flora. As well as plant specimens and leaf tissue samples, soil samples are collected, including bulk density samples and soil metagenomic samples.

The plant specimens are stored in Adelaide, South Australia and are available to loan for downstream research. The TERN Australia Soil and Herbarium Collection does not accept exchanges; however, we are in partnership with the State Herbarium of South Australia (AD) that do accept exchanges.

data.notes:
Entered Dec 2022.  Abbottabad is an important gateway to northern Pakistan and three mountain ranges, the Himalaya, Hindukush, and Karakuram. It is famous for its scenic beauty, moderate climate and educational institutions. 
The Herbarium was established by the Department of Botany in 1990. At that time, it was the only herbarium in the region. By 2005, the collection had grown to 10,000 specimens, but in October of that year, the area experienced devastating earthquake. The earthquake left many people dead or homeless and damaged much of the area’s infrastructure, including the herbarium. 
Fortunately, all involved decided that re-establishing and continuing to develop the area’s oldest and only herbarium was important. Consequently, space was set aside for the herbarium in the new BS building funded by the Saudi Government and the staff and students reorganized the surviving specimens in the new facility and began adding to them. By 2022, the collection had grown to 15,000 specimens and the decision was made to register it with Index herbariorum and to start sharing its holdings with the world via OpenHerbarium.

The Department of Botany started in 1958 with inception of degree courses under Kerala University under the leadership of Late Prof. K.V. George. In 1984, Post Graduate course was commenced and the department was elevated to the status of an approved research department affiliated to M.G. University in 2002.  This department is a pioneer department of St. Thomas College to  receive the DST-FIST grant in 2009.

The Department offers undergraduate programme in Botany based on CBCS syllabus and the sanctioned strength is 32. The post graduate programmes offered is based on CSS syllabus with Biotechnology  as specialization. Interdisciplinary/Open course is on Agri-based Microenterprises which is  good opportunity for other students to fulfill their passion towards botany, agriculture & horticulture. Botany Students study the Open Courses offered by other Departments.  Botany Complementary courses are offered for First and Second Year B. Sc Zoology students.   Short term courses offered by the department include Tissue culture for PG students and  Mushroom spawn production for UG students.

The Visayas State University Botanic Garden Herbarium (VSUBGH) was formally recognized as one of the core parts of the Zonal Center for Biodiversity Conservation and Habitat Restoration last February 2023. Although it's new, several collections were kept in the past years of continuous research on the native flora of the Visayas region in the Philippines, despite the global pandemic. With the institutionalization of the herbarium through Index Herbariorum, the project staff of the center would like to present its collections to a broader array of people in the region and globally. data.notes: Updated September 2022 (general update).  Mercer’s herbarium specimen data and living. collections are linked and managed using current BG-BASE software. Mercer’s vouchered herbarium specimens and/or living collections will support the Plant Collections Network, formerly, the North American Plant Collections Consortium of the American Public Gardens Association and currently support Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI) database.   In April 2014, the herbarium joined Mercer’s reference library, archives, laboratories and seed bank within Mercer’s newly-renovated research facility (~ 3,100 sf), the Mercer Botanical Center (MBC). The MBC provides additional dedicated space to accommodate expansion of the herbarium collections. In October 2016, the SBSC herbarium, botanical library and illustration collections were transferred to the Mercer Botanic Gardens as a long-term loan. Physical transfer of the SBSC collections was completed spring 2017 and the collections are available to researchers. Digitization of the SBSC collections is underway via NSF Grant 1902078. Mercer Botanic Gardens provides citizen scientist training programs for the Texas Master Gardener, Texas Master Naturalist, Texas Invaders, Native Plant Society of Texas, RBG Kew Millennium Seed Bank Training programs. The MERCA and SBSC herbarium collections support these education programs and facilitate training of herbarium volunteers. Mercer Botanic Gardens is a participating institution of The Center for Plant Conservation (headquartered at San Diego Zoo Global); is an affiliate of Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center; and is a member of the American Public Gardens Association and Botanic Gardens Conservation International.

data.notes: Updated January 2025. The specimens of the phanerogamic herbarium comes mainly from Italy (particularly from the South-Eastern Alps and the classical Karst regions) and the Mediterranean basin. Numerous samples also come from Europe, North America (Canada, United States), Japan, Canary Islands. There are also specimens used for the ""descriptio Florae Italiae"" of Pignatti (1982) and a rich collection of Genisteae, which was the subject of numerous systematic, chorological and palynological studies. The lichen samples come mostly from Italy and Europe as well as from non-European countries, particularly Asia: Armenia; Turkey (265 specimens); Russia, Altai mountains (390) and Lake Baikal (586); Japan (381), Alaska-Yukon (325), Northern Ontario (284), Svalbard Archipelago (102), Canary Islands (745), SW USA (1023), Mexico (512), Tierra del Fuego (452) and Antarctica (710). The lichenological herbarium is fully computerized and can be consulted at the link: https://italic.units.it/, dichotomic identification keys are also available. Algae specimens were collected mainly in the Mediterranean Basin (Adriatic Sea, Aegean Sea, Tyrrhenian Sea, Ligurian Sea, coasts around Sicily and Sardinia), but there are also samples coming from the Atlantic (North Sea and English and French coasts), Central-Southern Americas, African-Asian and Australian areas. The dichotomous identification keys of the Adriatic Sea algae can be found at the link: https://dryades.units.it/home/index.php?procedure=keys&organism%5B%5D=alg

data.associatedHerbaria: University of Dundee Botanic Garden, Riverside Drive, Dundee DD2 1QH
data.notes:
Updated January 2025 (general update).

The University of Dundee’s Herbarium contains over 15,000 plant specimens, including a large public collection of Angus flora, as well as comparative specimens from other parts of Scotland. It also has some more exotic plants from further afield, such as a fascinating 19th century collection of Darjeeling Ferns.
The Herbarium was begun by D'Arcy Thompson, Professor of Biology  at what was then University College Dundee, then developed by Patrick Geddes, the first Professor of Botany. Lack of resources forced Geddes to abandon his work on the collection, and only a few of the specimens that came to the University during his time survive today. The Herbarium does, however, contain many plant specimens from the 19th century, though these were acquired at a later date.
Following the gift of the Corstorphine Collection to the University in 1944, a later Botany lecturer, Dr Hugh Ingram, recommenced the active collection of herbarium specimens during the latter half of the 20th century. Various other researchers added to the collection until the decline of Botany teaching in the 1980s and 90s.
Updated Jan 2025 (contact email address).

data.associatedHerbaria: The University of Queensland
data.notes:
The CMLR herbarium is located at The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia and is a dedicated room with a large collection of plant specimens and plant identification resources such as powerful microscopes and a library of identification books. The herbarium contains up to 5,000 specimens as well an online digital herbarium which is a database containing high resolution scans of over 1,200 plant specimens. 
The herbarium is the only dedicated herbarium at The University of Brisbane and is a unique resource for researchers and students to confirm the identification of plant species related to land rehabilitation in Queensland, New South Wales and the Northern Territory. The herbarium also has one of the most comprehensive collections of species that are found in the endangered swamps of the Newnes Plateau (Western Blue Mountains region, New South Wales). The room contains an imaging microscope (Leica M205A) capable of high resolution magnification (160x), digital display, image capture, live measurements and multi-focus image stacking. The room is set at constant temperature (20°C) and humidity (45%) to maintain the preservation of plant samples.
Accurate plant identification is fundamental aspect of environmental surveys, particularly when studying the impacts of mining and the success of land rehabilitation. The herbarium is a place that researchers and students from around the university can work on plant identification, mount specimens for storage, or capture high resolution imagery of plant samples. 
Access to the digital herbarium is available through the CMLR home page and includes high resolution images of scanned specimens, maps of collections and links to online resources.  This digital herbarium is highly valuable to the mining industry, land managers, environmental scientists and plant enthusiasts, with a particular focus around the theme of land rehabilitation.

data.notes:
Updated Dec 2024 (specimen total).  Herbaria of Reunion island and of the Scattered Islands are hosted within the CBNM based in Reunion island. They contain samples of terrestrial vascular plants collected in different islands of the western Indian Ocean: Reunion, Europa, Juan de Nova, Glorioso and Tromelin. Among these are 5 834 specimens from Reunion Island and 2 909 from the Scattered Islands. These herbaria are completed by samples preserved in alcohol, by seed banks and by a collection in silica gel. 
Formal partnerships were established since 2014 with the National Museum of Natural History (P, Paris, France) and with the Missouri Botanical Garden (MO, Saint Louis, USA). In 2019, new partnerships have been created with the herbaria of Mayotte (MAO), Geneve (G) and Madagascar (TAN).
Since July 2016, data from the herbarium of the Scattered Islands are available online on Tropicos® (search by typing \'CBNM\' in the name of Senior Collector).
At the beginning of 2023, the project \\\'Establishment of a protocol for digitization and online sharing of parts of the Scattered Islands herbarium\\\' was accepted thanks to the call for projects \\\'Contribution to naturalist knowledge\\\' of the INPN. The phase of digitization of herbarium parts was thus able to be initiated thanks to the acquisition of equipment and the training of CBNM\\\'s agents. A digitization protocol is being drafted and will subsequently be applied to all of the CBNM\\\'s herbaria. The diffusion of very high resolution images and associated information will be done through a network of partners with online consultation platforms (e-ReColNat network, UMR PVBMT, Muséum National d\\\'Histoire Naturelle de Paris, IRD, Missouri Botanical Garden ).

data.taxonomicCoverage: Flowering Plants, Ferns and Fern Allies, Fungi
data.associatedHerbaria: Center of Excellence in Biodiversity and Natural Resource Management, University of Rwanda
data.notes:
The Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund International Herbarium is a unit of the Karisoke Research Center, a research institute and program of the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund in Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park. It was founded by Dian Fossey on 24 September 1967 to study endangered mountain gorillas. Fossey located the camp in Rwanda's Virunga volcanic mountain range, between Mount Karisimbi and Mount Bisoke, and named it by combining the names of the two mountains.

Today, Karisoke continues to upgrade its capacity for scientific research through new technology and new partnerships with local authorities and other conservation organizations. Recently, comedian Ellen DeGeneres plans to help build a permanent home in Rwanda for the work of the Fossey Fund to protect critically endangered mountain gorillas. The Ellen DeGeneres Campus of the Fossey Gorilla Fund is to be a permanent, specially designed facility for scientists who are helping to save mountain gorillas.

data.taxonomicCoverage: Fungi (non-lichenized and lichenized), Algae, Bryophyta, Vascular plants
data.geography: Poland (predominantly northeast part; Białowieża Primeval Forest)
data.notes:
Entered March 2022.  There are sections in the herbarium with independent specimen numbering, denoted by suffixes added to the main acronym: BLS M – theleomorphic fungi with macroscopic fructifications; BLS F – fungi with microscopic fructifications; BLS L – lichenized fungi; BLS A – algae, BLS B – bryophytes. Vascular plants are documented under acronym BLS without a suffix.
The herbarium includes one of the most representative collection of higher fungi (Ascomycota and Basidiomycota) from Białowieża Primeval Forest. The data about fungi with macroscopic fructifications are included in GBIF system.

data.quarantineRequirements: All incoming specimens are frozen for over two weeks.
data.notes: The herbarium includes many collections being a result of long-term studies conducted in Polish National Parks (Białowieża NP, Biebrza NP, Bieszczady NP, Kampinos NP, Wielkopolska NP), Western Sudety Mts, and specimens collected throughout the country by amateur mycologists within the project GREJ (Database of Rare and Endangered Fungi of Poland; https://grzyby.pl/rejestr-grzybow-chronionych-i-zagrozonych.htm). The most important collections are coprinoid fungi (ca. 3 000 specimens), Tulostoma (ca. 450 specimens), and Lepiota s.l. (ca. 1 500 specimens).

 The herbarium is currently arranged according to Bentham & Hooker's system, although a rearrangement based on APG-III has been initiated.  Arya Vaidya Sala, Kottakkal has been maintaining a demonstration Garden of 8 acres with a live collection of more than thousand species of medicinal plants. Rare species like <Utleria salicifolia>, <Janakiya arayalpatra>, <Decalepis hamiltonii>, <Rauvolfia serpentina>, <Embelia ribes>, <Coscinium fenestratum> etc. are conserved here. Entered Jan 2019.  The Botanical Collection of Medicinal Plants, CBPM, was established with the support from the Institute of Pharmaceutical Technology (Farmanguinhos) / Fiocruz. It aims to ensure the botanical identification and traceability of plant species of medical interest in order to facilitate secure access and rational use of medicinal plants and herbal medicines, promoting the sustainable use of biodiversity and the development of Science, Techonology & Inovation projects related to drugs from plant origin, in accordance with the precepts of the National Policy of Medical Plants and Herbal Medicines (Política Nacional de Plantas Medicinais e Fitoterápicos - PNPMF).
The herbarium is registered in the Brazilian Herbaria Network formed from the "Herbaria Comission" of Brazil Botanical Society (Sociedade Botânica do Brasil - SBB) and is part of the Agroecological Platform of Phytomedicine (Plataforma Agroecológica de Fitomedicamentos -PAF) from the Management Center for Biodiversity and Health (Núcleo de Gestão em Biodiversidade e Saúde - NGBS) - Farmanguinhos / Fiocruz. The CBPM is dedicated to collecting, georeferencing, storage, exchange, preservation and botanical identification of medicinal plants, as well as providing advisory services in the areas of botany, ethnobotany and pharmacobotany to meet the institutions whose projects are registered in the PAF.

As well, the collection houses many voucher specimens for Dr. McLean’s research into Thesium ramosum Hayne (Thesiaceae), and Macdonald’s research on the vascular plant floras of 1) the LaCloche Mountains (Ontario); 2) the City of Terre Haute (Indiana); 3) the Rattray’s Marsh Conservation Area (Ontario). 

    The herbarium collection currently represents157 Families, 742 Genera and 2493 Species.

    The current accessioned collections are from the following jurisdictions: Ontario (1050 specimens), Alberta (1005), Indiana (431), Saskatchewan (372), British Columbia (332), Montana (212), Manitoba (156), and the remainder are from across the continent.

    As well, there are well over 1,000 additional collections representing an additional over 200 species waiting for processing and official accessioning into the herbarium.

data.geography:
The phycological herbarium is housed at the División Ficología “Dr. Sebastián A. Guarrera”. It holds about 17,000 specimens/samples, mostly microalgae, both marine and freshwater, inventoried since 1969. The herbarium includes the type materials of 506 taxa.
Besides recent and contemporary microalgae collections, the herbarium is house of historical diatom collections. Of them, the collection gathered by Frenguelli, pioneer of diatom studies in South America, is the most relevant. The Frenguelli Diatom Collection (FDC) constitutes a primary reference for worldwide diatomists since it allows access to information on diatom biodiversity extending back up to 100 years ago. The FDC represents the biodiversity existing in the past as it gathers samples from South America (Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Bolivia and Peru) and Antarctica. Additional gatherings from Italy, Egypt and Somalia also make up the collection.
Frenguelli ́s legacy also includes two worldwide known reference diatom collections: 
-“Collection Tempère et Peragallo (Diatomées du Monde Entier, 2e. Édition)” consists of a set of 1000 slides containing diatom assemblages from c. 900 localities, fossil or recent, freshwater and marine, from different parts of the world. Complete sets of slides are rare, housed in a few research institutions in Europe and USA. Presently, an almost complete set (995 of 1000 slides) of this collection is curated at the Herbarium LPC
-“Möller Collection” consists of 117 slides with strews of mixed diatom species, 5 slides of “Diatomaceen Typen-Platte” and 2 slides of “Diatomaceen Probe-Platte”. Both Typen- and  Probe-Platten are accompanied by an explanatory brochure. 
The Herbarium also houses more recent collections gathered by the following collectors:
- S.A. Guarrera: freshwater microalgae from different areas of Argentina, mainly from Patagonia and Pampasic regions.
-M.E. Ferrario: marine phytoplankton from Antarctica and Southwestern Atlantic Ocean.
-A. Boltovskoy: freshwater phytoplankton, mainly dinoflagellates, from different regions of Argentina.
-S. Cabrera: macroalgae from coastal Buenos Aires province and Patagonia.

data.notes:
The National Herbarium (NH) was established in 1998 
with financial support from the Danish International 
Development Agency (DANIDA) and became operational 
in 2003. It is the only herbarium in the country 
(Herbarium code THIM) listed in the Index Herbariorum 
 (https://sweetgum.nybg.org/science/ih/) - a guide to the 
world’s herbaria and where only those collections that 
are permanent scientific repositories are included.
The main functions of the National Herbarium are to 
serve as the national repository of “Type” (A preserved 
specimen designated as a permanent reference for a 
new species, new genus or some other taxon) and 
voucher specimens of botanical collections; lead and 
coordinate plant systematics and taxonomy-related 
studies, including national floristic works; and identify 
conservation priority species in the country. The ancillary 
functions include providing taxonomic services to other 
agencies and stakeholders. and programs of the centres.
Over the past 20 years, the National Herbarium focussed 
on building its collections through routine collections 
programs, international collaborations and national 
thematic projects, including the (i) Bhutan fern project, 
(ii) Pilot project on invasive plant species of Bhutan, 
(iii) 
Comprehensive assessment of climate change impacts 
on endemic plant diversity, (iv) Impact assessment of 
invasive plants in Bhutan, (v) Red listing of Bhutan’s 
endemic plant species, and 
(vi) Biodiversity conservation 
and sustainable use in High Altitude Northern Areas of 
Bhutan (HANAs). Currently, the NH houses 
approximately 19,309 accessions of Angiosperms, 
Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, and Bryophytes 
specimens.

data.notes:
Department of Botany and Microbiology is the one of the oldest departments in the university. The department has a big herbarium, Garhwal University Herbarium. This herbarium is recognized internationally. The acronym GUH has been assigned to it which is registered in Index herbariorum at New York, U.S.A. The GUH contains about 20,000 plant specimens of various plant groups like Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Lichens, and Fungi. 
The herbarium is a repository of our plant wealth and need day to day maintenance, and plant identification is a time-consuming process. This facility is used for taxonomical studies leading to writing the flora of a region or other floristic and ecological notes on the Himalayan plants. The structure or organization of Garhwal University Herbarium is based on Bentham and Hooker’s system of classification. The preserved specimens in this herbarium include a large number of medicinal, aromatic and other economic plants from Western Himalayan region is very well represented. Besides technical details, habit, habitat, flowering and fruiting time of every specimen has been recorded in this herbarium for making it a ready reference and for use by the herbal drug industry for authentication of plant material.

data.notes:
WII Herbarium: A National Repository - represents flora of a number of Protected Areas of India
The scientific value of herbaria as a botanical repository of Earth's current and past diversity is globally acknowledged. The Wildlife Institute of India Herbarium, recognized by the ""Index Herbariorum,"" is listed among the 3567 network of herbaria worldwide cited using the acronym ""WII"" in the scientific and botanical publications.

WII Herbarium was established in 1986 with a twofold purpose: (i) to create a repository of plant collections representing flora of different Protected Areas (PAs) of India and (ii) to develop a basic facility for aiding plant identification, floral inventory and access to plant databases for officer trainees, researchers, and students of WII.

One of unique features of WII herbarium is that it represents flora of a number of protected areas of India. Based on the floristic surveys and inventory of species, the database on the flora of protected areas namely Asola Bhatti Wildlife Sanctuary, Bandhavgarh National Park, Grasslands in and around Pachmarhi Wildlife Sanctuary, Bodhghat submergence area, Madhya Pradesh, Great Himalayan National Park, Pin Valley National Park, Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary, Valley of Flowers National Park, Cold­arid region of Nanda Devi BR, Rajaji National Park, Eravikulam National Park, Protected areas of Andhra Pradesh, Jaldapara Wildlife Sanctuary, Gorumara National Park, Hemis National Park, Dachigam National Park, Rann of Kutch, Pakhui Wildlife Sanctuary, Arunachal Pradesh etc. has been prepared.

data.notes: O herbário foi idealizado em 2006 pelos estudantes e docentes do Departamento de Engenharia Florestal da Universidade Federal dos Vales do Jequitinhonha e Mucuri com finalidade de subsidiar as disciplinas deste curso, oferecer suporte aos estudos de vegetação e consequentemente congregar coleções científicas da flora regional. Em 2011 o acervo tomou proporções consideráveis sendo necessárias melhorias na forma de armazenamento e novas estruturas e equipamentos foram adquiridos. Nesta época o herbário recebeu a denominação Herbário Dendrológico Jeanine Felfili, com a sigla oficial HDJF, bem como o reconhecimento oficial junto à Rede Brasileira de Herbários e ao Index Herbariorum. O acervo HDJF está dividido em três partes, a saber: material herborizado; xiloteca e carpoteca. Todo o acervo está condicionado em uma área física de 66 m², com projeto de expansão aguardando recursos financeiros para tanto. O acervo do HDJF está compilado em bando de dados e as suas exsicatas estão sendo digitalizadas a fim de serem disponibilizadas online. O HDJF está inserido na porção Meridional da Serra do Espinhaço, fitogeograficamente a região que apresenta um complexo mosaico de florestas estacionais e savana, com diversas fitofisonomias relativamente bem preservadas, sendo considerada área prioritária para conservação e investigação científica. Assim no acervo tem destaque para a flora regional com exemplares dos biomas Mata Atlântica e Cerrado, contudo há também representação de outros biomas como Amazônia e Caatinga, oriundos do programa de permutas de duplicatas e intercâmbio com outros herbários.

data.notes: The Herbarium of the department of Botany, Sri Krishnadevaraya University, Ananthapuramu (formerly Anantapur) with an acronym ‘SKU’ is the largest herbarium in Andhra Pradesh and the second largest in South Indian Universities. It was started in 1983 by Prof. T. Pullaiah and later from 1996 onwards Dr. B. Ravi Prasad Rao is the in-charge  for SKU. SKU houses about 45,000+ specimens collected during 1983-2025 from different parts of states of Andhra Pradesh and  Telangana and other states of Southern Peninsular India and Andaman Islands. These specimens represent different plant groups: algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms. There are 17 type specimens in SKU. All the specimens are preserved by dry and wet method using rectified spirit and mercuric chloride and guaranteed to exist without any damage for about a century. Duplicates of these specimens as well field notes are being maintained separately in the herbarium store room. Chief contributors are  Prof. T. Pullaiah team (about 11,000 specimens)  Prof. R.R. Venkata Raju (1800) and Prof. B. Ravi Prasad Rao team (about +31, 500). Most of the collections are made with the support of national funding agency supported research projects like UGC, DST, CSIR and DBT. About 20,000 specimens are collected from Eastern Ghats and 3500 from Andaman Islands. Specimens are arranged in specially designed cupboards following Angiosperm Phylogeny Group classification (APG IV, 2016) . Prof. B. Ravi Prasad Rao is the Director of the herbarium and can be contacted at biodiversityravi@gmail.com for more information.

Updated Jan 2023:
In the morning of 10 October 2022, the historical center of the City of Kyiv was hit by several russian missiles. As result, the historical buildings of the M.G. Kholodny Institute of Botany NAS of Ukraine and the National Herbarium of Ukraine (KW) were hit by the shock waves. Both buildings were hit by the shock waves and some fragments of missiles or damaged structures. About 20 windows were destroyed or severely damaged and was discovered several roof leaks (the holes were caused by the missile fragments). In particular, the ceiling in the Lesser Herbarium Hall has been damaged.  Currently, the urgent repair of the buildings has been completed, but the repair of the damage is ongoing.  (Detail report please see: https://ukrbotj.co.ua/archive/79/5/339). 

Updated Nov 2022:
An update from the KW Herbarium and our Institute: We were planning to start tomorrow (Wednesday) the serious repair and replacement of windows (damaged during the 10 October 2022 missile strikes) at the Institute of Botany and KW National Herbarium, but now it is hardly possible because the windows company will not be able to work under unstable power supply. The works will be most probably postponed.

Updated Oct 2022:
Email message received from Dr. Sergei Mosyakin, Director of the M. G. Kholodny Institute of Botany on 10 October 2022, reporting on damage  to KW during the recent Russian airstrikes:  Mostly windows, roofs, some non-critical structures. Anyway, some serious renovation will be needed before the winter. Right now, no irreversible loss of specimens, no harm to our staff. Our people who today worked here, did some basic repair and cleared the mess are fantastic. 

Updated January 2022.
In addition to the main part, which contains materials of vascular plants, the Herbarium KW includes some important parts (subdivisions) that have a unique abbreviation: KW-M (Mycology Herbarium – Herbarium of Fungi and Fungi-like Organisms), KW-L (Lichen Herbarium), KW-B( Bryophyte herbarium), KW-A (Algotheca), KW-P (Palynotheca). 
No specimens are currently available for sending on loan; however, images are provided upon request, if available. The exchange of specimens is temporarily unavailable due to changed governmental regulations.

data.herbariumName: Herbarium of the International Dendrological Foundation (IDFHU)
data.exchangeAvailable: Duplicates from Mexico, northern North America, Central Europe, Central Asia
data.notes:
Entered Oct 2024.

IDFHU is located near Székesfehérvár, Fejér County in the Amádé-Bajzáth-Pappenhein mansion in the village of Iszkaszentgyörgy. It is surrounded by a 5 ha park and parkforest.
The herbarium and corresponding botanical exhibit and library occupy 430 m2 in 13 rooms and contains around 250 ,000 plant samples from 89800 different accessions, with particular emphasis on conifers and woody elements of the coniferous forests of Earth’s
temperate climate zones. 
 
History: goes back to 1971 when the Dendrological Documentation Project (DDP) was launched by Dr. Zsolt Debreczy at the Botanical Department of the Natural History
Museum in Budapest. Soon after when he and botanical illustrator Dr. Vera Csapody
published the applied-botanical book, “Gardens Green in Winter Too” in 1971, 
they realized the importance of the parallel study and documentation of wild- collected, and authentic cultivated specimens for morphological comparison. A research team with Dr. István Rácz and Dr. Gyöngyvér Biró was organized for photo documentation and library research, respectively, and several botanical illustrators contributed to the work.

From 1988-1991 the team continued its work at the Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University
and subsequently at the Massachusetts- based International Dendrological Research Institute, Inc. (I.D.R.I.), with the close collaboration of the non-profit organization Earthwatch, Inc. (EW). In 1995 Zsolt Debreczy left the Natural History Museum (BP) and has started to develop I.D.R.I.’s herbarium, which became the foundation of IDFHU’s current extensive collection.
 
Expeditions: in collaboration with EW (1991-1997) a worldwide documentation project
started with the assistance of 165 EW volunteers, and the subsequent research and documentation eventually covered the entire temperate zones in both Hemispheres.

Location: In 1999, for logistical reasons, IDRI’s rapidly growing herbarium moved into a 650 m2 building in Budakeszi, next to Budapest, and then, in 2023 to its current, even more ideal location. 

Complementary collections: fruit, seed and extensive cone (2800 pieces); wood collections (ca. 1000 samples); photograph collection (350 000 negatives and transparencies, partially scanned); original drawings (botanical artwork) created for ‘Conifers around the World I-II’ and the Dendrological Atlas (Conifers and other gymnosperms of the temperate climate zones and adjacent regions, in preparation). 

Contact: 
Dr. István Rácz, Curator; 
Dr. Zsolt Debreczy, Curator and Research Director, founder of the International Dendrological Foundation;
Timea Kleszken, Asst. Herb. Curator

The Fielding Herbarium contains all non-British material collected by former Department of Botany staff since 1769, and since it was largely obtained through purchase of material at auctions in the early 19th century, it is particularly rich in type material. The Druce Herbarium contains all British phanerogams that were collected later than 1769.  The history of OXF has been comprehensively studied by H. M. data.notes: The Biota Collection Room at Universitas Indonesia was initially established on the Depok campus to support the Plant Taxonomy Practicum Course and was pioneered by Amril Djalil, who led the plant taxonomy research lab and reference collection facility from 1987. Early students collected plant specimens from fieldwork in Greater Jakarta and western part of Java, gradually expanding the collection to cover various regions in Indonesia. After Drs. Amril Djalil's retirement in 2007, activity in the herbarium declined until revitalization efforts were initiated in 2018 by Mega Atria, Alexander Tianara, and Afiatry Patrika. Now known as the Herbarium Depokensis (UIDEP), this educational herbarium is a key resource in Universitas Indonesia's botanical studies, focusing on urban floras.

data.notes: Established in 2023, the herbarium houses an estimated 4,650 curated specimens representing the flora of Southern Brazil, with emphasis on the Central-Southern region of Paraná State. The collection focuses on vascular plants from the Araucaria Forest (Floresta Ombrófila Mista) and associated ecosystems. Holdings include specimens of threatened taxa and type material of species currently under formal description. The herbarium also preserves vouchers documenting significant regional distribution records. The collection supports research in taxonomy, systematics, reproductive biology, and biodiversity conservation, contributing to long-term documentation of Southern Brazilian flora.

data.associatedHerbaria: Mardin Artuklu University
data.notes:
Entered Jan 2024.  Mardin Artuklu University Herbarium aims to detect, document, and collect all plant samples, including common, rare, endemic, food, ornamental, medicinal, and poisonous plant taxa, to preserve the plant diversity database of Mardin province.
Mardin province has a rich biodiversity due to the presence of Mediterranean, continental, and desert climates and the altitude between the mountain and the plain parts. Mardin province and its surroundings are among the ancient locations that have been adopted by humanity since the earliest periods of history. The fossil records show the use of plants dates to the Middle Palaeolithic period, approximately 60 000 years ago. Eight different plant species were identified on a human corpse found in 1960 in the Shanidar cave, which is very close to the province of Mardin. However, the historically rich plant biodiversity of Mardin province is under threat due to various reasons, such as the unconscious use of pesticides, the construction of dams and ponds, excessive and uncontrolled grazing, concretion and destruction of green areas, and industrial facilities. Therefore, documentation of floristic composition and preserving dried plant samples grown in Mardin province have significant importance in terms of biodiversity and plant conservation.

Entered Jan 2020.  Mustafa Kemal University Plant Protection Department (MKUBK) was established in 1993. Department is giving both academic education and research activities with 15 full-time Professors, Associate Professor and Research assistant. Especially Plant Mycology and Bacteriology labs are collecting several disease samples not only from the region but also from different parts of Turkey. 
In 2017, Centre for Implementation and Research of Plant Health Clinic (MKU-BISAK) was established officially as part of the Plant Protection Department to help producers (farmers) for identification and giving advice to farmers from all around from Turkey. 
Each year, Bsc, Msc and PhD students working on plant pathogenic fungi and bacteria collect several infected plant samples, isolate  and identify causal disease agents from diseased samples. In centre, all disease agents are either kept as herbaria on its host plants or isolated microbial culture on nutrient media. 
BİSAK maintains several plant pathogenic fungi and bacterial culture collections (published or unpublished) in its centre. This center also giving services to anyone who wants to identify their fungal and bacterial agents. Center has more than 500 samples

data.taxonomicCoverage: Medicinal, poisonous, food plant, fungi, algae and lichen samples
data.notes:
Eastern Anatolia is the largest (approximately 170 000 km2) of seven geographical divisions of Turkey with 14 provinces, bordering Iraq, Iran, Nakhichevan, Armenia, and Georgia. It is included in the Irano-Turanian phytogeographical region, covered with deciduous-mixed forests and deciduous tree steppes. The area is surrounded by coastal mountain ranges, which protects it from the moderating effect of sea breezes. Subsequently, the winters are cold and long, with snow lasting for several months. They are followed by very short and rainy springs, and hot and dry summers. The mountainous and strongly fragmentised area offers numerous microclimatic and ecological zones, which provided suitable conditions for the development of diverse flora.
      The local population has a comprehensive knowledge of traditional herbal medicines which are commonly used to prevent or to treat disease. This knowledge was developed over centuries, when Eastern Anatolia served as a passageway between the continents of Europe, Asia and Africa. A variety of flora, fauna and cultures owe their geographical spread to this passageway. Over many centuries a number of races and tribes originated from distant lands settled in Eastern Anatolia, bringing knowledge of plants and their various uses. This heritage, combined with the local flora, has contributed to an extensive use of plants in daily life as a medicine. The knowledge of herbal medicines in this region is still mostly passed on orally (with the exception of a few codices) from one generation of religious healers (referred to as‘seyh’) and local healers (‘hekim’) to the next.

data.notes: Entered Sep 2024.  The PLM Herbarium (PLMH) is a university-based herbarium located at Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila (PLM), Intramuros, Philippines, dedicated to preserving plant and fungal specimens primarily gathered from undergraduate research projects and course requirements since 1983. The collection includes approximately 500-600 specimens housed in the university’s biology laboratory, representing various taxa such as algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms, fungi, and lichens. The primary objective of PLMH is to serve as a repository for specimens collected by student researchers and faculty members, supporting education, research, and citizen science initiatives with a focus on benefiting the academic community and the residents of Manila.

data.notes:
Entered Feb 2025.  The Herbarium HCSP is a significant botanical collection that serves as a vital resource for research, conservation, and education. Established with the contributions of renowned botanist Dr. Daniel Montesinos, the herbarium currently houses over 1,500 species meticulously collected by him throughout Peru. Additionally, it contains more than 1,000 specimens gathered by students, reflecting a collaborative effort to document the country’s rich biodiversity.

One of the most valuable aspects of the HCSP collection is the presence of isotypes, paratypes, and neotypes, particularly within the Caryophyllaceae and Asteraceae families. Dr. Montesinos' collections are highly regarded due to their broad geographic range and scientific accuracy, making them critical references for taxonomic and ecological studies. These specimens not only contribute to the understanding of Peru’s flora but also serve as an essential repository for researchers working on plant systematics and conservation.

The HCSP Herbarium continues to expand, fostering botanical research and providing an invaluable resource for students, scientists, and conservationists dedicated to the study of plant diversity in Peru.

data.notes: The herbarium of Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park (CHOH) was formally established and organized in 2025. Collections include botanical surveys from researchers and collections from National Park Service personnel. All specimens from the herbarium were collected within the legislative boundary of C&O Canal NHP, an area of 184.5 miles along the Potomac River between Cumberland, MD and Washington DC. The focus of this herbarium is to demonstrate the diverse floral resources of the park to the public and with special emphasis on state rare, threatened, and endangered plant species. The CHOH Herbarium functions as a reference collection of herbarium specimens which supports taxonomic, systematic, biogeographic, ecological, and conservation biological research.

Vale do Araguaia Herbarium (HERVA)
Affiliated with the Federal University of Mato Grosso – Araguaia Campus, the Vale do Araguaia Herbarium (HERVA) is dedicated to documenting and preserving the plant diversity of the Vale do Araguaia region, a transitional zone between the Cerrado, Amazon, and Pantanal biomes.
The collection is composed primarily of specimens from the regional flora, with emphasis on species from forest and savanna formations. These collections contribute to advancing taxonomic, ecological, and phytogeographical knowledge of the region.
HERVA supports teaching, research, and outreach activities, serving as a reference center for floristic, phytosociological, ecological, and vegetation conservation studies.

data.associatedHerbaria: BLS Białystok University of Technology in Hajnówka, Poland; BIL Herbarium of Department of Natural Forests FRI in  Bialowieza PL
data.notes:
Entered Jan 2026.  History of the herbarium  
The herbarium collection was created primarily as a result of research projects in which the identification of species collected in the field required laboratory conditions. Appropriate permits were obtained for collecting protected species or material gathered within protected areas, and the responsibility for their storage rests with the executing institution – the Forest Research Institute. The main specialists who identified the specimens are:
- Vascular plants: J. Czerepko, R. Gawryś, O. Hrynyk, K. Lipińska, P. Marciniuk, W. Pisarek
- Bryophytes and lichens: C. Cacciatori, W. Ciurzycki, J. Czerepko, W. Fałtynowicz, R. Gawryś, M. Kukwa, A. Łubek, A. Obidziński, D. Skowron, A. Stebel, R. Szymczyk, W. Pisarek
The herbarium was established in 2007 on the initiative of Janusz Czerepko, an employee of the Forest Research Institute in Sękocin Stary (Poland). Significant contributions to the preparation of the collection and storage facilities were made by: Radosław Gawryś, Kateryna Lipińska, Olena Hrynyk, and Julia Sochacka.

Nature and scientific significance of the collection  
The herbarium documents the diversity of forest flora in Poland, with particular emphasis on bryophytes, epiphytes, epixylic species, and vascular plants representing forest habitats. The collection is used in:

- forest ecology research,
- biodiversity analyses,
- documentation of habitat changes,
- projects related to species conservation and ecosystem monitoring.

Cataloguing system  
The catalogue is maintained in both paper and digital form.
Each specimen is accompanied by a label containing e.g. information on location, date, and collector.

Storage conditions  
The collection is stored in metal cabinets.
Regular inspection and low‑temperature sterilization are carried out.
The storage room maintains stable microclimatic conditions.

Access to the collection  
Access for researchers is possible upon prior arrangement.
Specimen loans are available upon agreement.

The total number of species in the herbarium is 940, including 13 ferns, 4 clubmosses, 6 horsetails, 578 flowering plants, as well as 200 bryophytes and 139 lichens.

data.notes:
Entered Jan 2026.  The Manuel de Arruda Câmara Herbarium (Acronym HACAM) is a scientific collection linked to the Department of Biology of the State University of Paraíba (UEPB), in Campina Grande Paraíba State, Brazil. Founded with the aim of supporting teaching, research and university extension, HACAM works in the conservation of plant biodiversity, especially the northeastern flora, with emphasis on the Caatinga and the Atlantic Forest.
Its collection is mainly made up of exsiccatae (pressed and dried plants), covering a wide diversity of botanical families, collected in different regions of the state of Paraíba and the Brazilian Northeast and other countries (Bolivia, Paraguay, Portugal, and Germany). The herbarium plays a fundamental role in the identification, cataloging and study of plant species, being a regional reference in floristics, plant taxonomy and plant systematics.
In addition to being a space for scientific research, HACAM is also dedicated to the training of human resources, welcoming undergraduate and graduate students in internship activities, scientific initiation and extension projects. The herbarium is also an important center of exchange with other institutions, actively participating in the national network of herbaria (such as the INCT-Virtual Herbário da Flora e dos Fungos) and maintaining partnerships with several research centers in Brazil.
Founded in September 1981 by Professor Ivan Coelho Dantas, with Professor José Iranildo Miranda de Melo as its current curator, HACAM is one of the five herbaria in the State of Paraíba, and the only one in the immediate region of Campina Grande. The name of the herbarium honors Manuel de Arruda Câmara (1752–1810), a naturalist and botanist from Paraíba, a pioneer in scientific studies on Brazilian flora during the colonial period. His trajectory represents the spirit of scientific curiosity and appreciation of knowledge about Brazilian nature that also inspires the work done at HACAM.

data.notes:
Entered Mar 2026.  The National Mushroom Center (NMC) has developed extensive experience in production and marketing of edible and medicinal mushrooms. The National Mushroom Centre (NMC) is based in Wanchutaba, Thimphu. The Centre staff report directly to the Department of Agriculture.

One of the primary activities of the Centre is to develop a National Fungorum from collecting wild mushrooms, identifying the specimens and drying the fungi specimens for preservation. Currently, more than 2350 fungi specimens including poisonous, edible, and medicinal fungi have been collected. Specimen data is databased and specimens are digitally imaged with data published in a publicly available specimen data portal. The fungi collection is being expanded through additional field expeditions and collecting throughout Bhutan.

In 2017, the national herbarium received assistance from Dr. Michael B. Thomas through a partnership with the US Fulbright program. This collaboration led to the databasing and specimen workflow development for the fungi specimen collecting led by Sabitra Pradham and subsequent specimen data portal development. Since 2017, Dr. Thomas has continued to serve as the fungi Data Curator and assist in capacity building and database training.

data.notes: Updated April 2026: The Somali Region Livestock and Agricultural Research Institute (SoRLARI) is the leading regional institution dedicated to advancing livestock, agriculture, and natural resource research across the Somali Region of Ethiopia. The foundation of the SoRLARI Herbarium dates back to 1992–1993, when the South East Rangeland Development Project undertook extensive plant specimen collection across the region. This initiative aimed to systematically identify, document, and preserve representative plant species, creating a scientific baseline for biodiversity and rangeland studies. Following completion of the project, the herbarium collection was formally transferred to SoRLARI, where it has been maintained and expanded as a permanent scientific repository. Today, the herbarium plays a critical role in supporting research in taxonomy, ecology, conservation biology, and sustainable natural resource management. A digitisation project starting in 2026 aims to make this collection more widely accessible.

Important collectors also include students and researchers from the Forestry Engineering School at Universidad Nacional de Cajamarca, as well as biologists involved in the conservation of protected natural areas in northern Peru.

The current herbarium originated from the former PPEA herbarium, established in 1985 and closed in 1990. The collection was later transferred to the Faculty and subsequently incorporated into the Forestry Engineering School at Universidad Nacional de Cajamarca in 1993. Botanical collections continued intermittently thereafter, with continuous new accessions from 2004 onward.

The herbarium is currently under development within the Forestry Engineering School and focuses on documenting and preserving the vascular plant diversity of northern Peru, particularly Andean forest ecosystems. It supports academic training, botanical research, and biodiversity conservation initiatives, with the aim of serving as a regional reference collection.

Scope: The Flora and Lichenized Mycobiota of New Zealand. UNITEC has an emphasis on the northern part of New Zealand particularly the lichens of the Kermadec Islands, Northland, Kaipara (Mataia), Waitakere Ranges, urban Auckland, Auckland Regional Parks, Hauraki Gulf Islands (notable collections from Rangitoto, Motukaikoura and Tiritirimatangi), Waikato and Chatham Islands. Herbarium collections also reflect participation in Auckland Bioblitz (Auckland Domain, Auckland Botanical Gardens, Dingle Dell, Kepa Bush/Pourewa, Miranda, Smiths Bush, and Twin Streams (Opanuku Stream Catchment)). Invasive plants are also well represented reflecting staff research interests e.g., Taraxacum, and the courses taught by the facility.

The herbarium also holds DNA vouchers linked to the Applied Molecular Solutions Research Group (http://www.unitec.ac.nz/ams) and associated laboratory, and international lichen research consortia (PhyloRamalina, Lecanomics, Parsys).

The earliest collections are those donated collections from 1965 (Judy Nicholson, mainly South Island), with other later donations from the 1980s and 1990s, before active collecting began in 2001.

History: UNITEC was founded by Carol Elliott (nee Lockett) and Dan Blanchon in 2001. It is a teaching and research herbarium, with a major strength in New Zealand lichens, and which supports the research of an active lichen research group, as well as research on invasive and indigenous species.  Students learn herbarium specimen collection and preparation in three different courses in the Bachelor and Masters of Applied Science, and students volunteer in the herbarium to assist with accessioning and curation. The herbarium supports taxonomy education, particularly in lichenology, mycology, botany and biosecurity.

The main lichen collections of New Zealand Lichenologists Dan Blanchon, Andrew Marshall and Peter de Lange are held at UNITEC (including important lichen collections from the Kermadec and Chatham Islands, and northern New Zealand).

data.notes:
Updated May 2026
Updated Sep 2017 (name of the institution updated).  The Herbarium of Vale do Taquari (HVAT Herbarium) is linked to the Museum of Sciences Univates of University of  Vale do Taquari - Univates. The Museum has started its activities in 1995 with the formalization of an agreement with the city of Lajeado, when it installed the Botanical Garden of the city, with the objective to record the species existing in that space. With the closing of the agreement, the first name (Herbarium Lajeado Botanical Garden - HJBL) was replaced by HUNIVATES and later by the current name. Since then, the Herbarium has the legacy to support the documentation of regional plant diversity and the availability of this information to the scientific and general community. The herbarium is part of the Brazilian Network Herbarium and the Rio Grande do Sul Herbarium Network, and is connected to SpeciesLink network. The Herbarium of Vale do Taquari has also integrated INCT Virtual Herbarium of Flora and Fungi during the period of the project. The collection, organized according to the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group III system, is fully computerized using the software database Jabot and available online at SpeciesLink. The samplings are originated from 15 Brazilian states, being most of them from the southern of Brazil, representative two of the existing biomes in Rio Grande do Sul (Pampa and Atlantic Forest). Considering the phytoecological formations, the most representative is the species that make up the Deciduous Forest of the Atlantic Forest biome, plant formation where the region of your location is located. The records of the species are distributed in 179 families, being Asteraceae the most representative, followed by Orchidaceae, Poaceae, Fabaceae, among others. It should be noted that the species of the Orchidaceae family are well represented in the Herbarium, constituting one of the largest collections of this family in Rio Grande do Sul.

data.notes:
(last update: May 2025)
FI includes a number of sub-collections, either open to further improvement, or closed (""historical herbaria""); each of them is listed as a separate entry in GRSciColl (https://scientific-collections.gbif.org/), where further details are provided. The largermost of these sub-collections are the General Herbarium (FI-GEN), which incorporated the Herbarium libycum (15,000 specimens), the Philip Barker Webb's herbarium (Herbarium webbianum, FI-W), the Odoardo Beccari's Malesian herbarium (Herbarium beccarianum, FI-HB), the Micheli-Targioni herbarium (Herbarium michelianum, FI-M), the Rodolfo Emilio Giuseppe Pichi Sermolli's herbarium (Herbarium pichianum, FI-PS) and the Odoardo Beccari's palms herbarium (Herbarium palmarum, FI-HP).  The Botanical collections also includes a number of important, historical herbaria, such as the Andrea Cesalpino's and the Tuscan anonymous' herbaria (FI-CES and FI-MER, respectively, both dating backs to 16th century), and several ancillary collections (seeds, fruits, wood samples etc.). Due to the historical significance and uniqueness of most collections, physical loan is only possible for a limited number of FI-GEN and the ancillary collections specimens. A large, comprehensive digitization project led by the Padova University, thanks to the National Biodiversity Future Center (NBFC) initiative and through the Next Generation EU and Italian National Resistance and Resilience Programme (PNRR) fundings,  has started in March 2024 into the herbarium rooms, aiming to the complete databasing and imaging of FI and other important Italian herbaria.

data.notes: Updated June 2026. The regional collection, traditionally known as "Rheinisches Herbar" (Rhenish Herbarium), has been curated by BONN since 1973, but was separated as an independent herbarium in 1998 (as NHV). The owner of the collection is the Leibniz Institute for the Analysis of Biodiversity Change (LIB), located in Bonn, Germany. The non-Rheinanian part of the herbarium, called "Ausserrheinisches Herbar" (210 000 specimens), was transferred to Berlin-Dahlem in 1936 (but kept outside, thus surviving the 1943 fire), taken to Russia by the Soviet army after World War II, returned in due course to East Berlin (BHU), and eventually reintegrated into B in 1993. The remaining Rhenish Herbarium (NHV, ~70 000 specimens) has been housed at the LIB in Bonn since 2026.
